Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

BitChat is not a covert network. It is a Bluetooth mesh: nearby phones form a local cluster, and a message hops through other phones about seven hops, a few hundred metres in good conditions. No account. No phone number. No central server. Direct messages are end-to-end encrypted. Built for a crowd, a protest, a blackout, a disaster zone. Not city-wide messaging.
The public record of misuse is thin. The documented Indian spike is July 2026, around the Jantar Mantar protests. India briefly accounted for most of the app’s global downloads. The official line was “substantial risk of misuse.” No reported case of a serious offence is in the open record.
Police cannot do with this what they do with WhatsApp or a telecom operator. That fear can exist. It is not evidence the app has been used for a serious crime in India.
Section 69A lets the Centre order an intermediary to block public access to information on grounds such as security or public order. Apple’s notice says MeitY used it because the app “includes content that is illegal in India.” It does not name that content. The order has not been published.
The Court upheld 69A in Shreya Singhal only with safeguards: written reasons, a committee, a hearing, and a path to court. A secret whole-app removal is a different design.
Blocking the app, in secret, because it still works when the network is cut, is not the same as blocking a specific unlawful message. 🔪📵⚖️

Yesterday, Trump declared a national emergency over the power grid. People are concerned it's a setup to take the grid down. That's where we are at with trust in our government. So let's look at what it actually is, how it WOULD help a grid takedown if that's the goal, and whether it really looks like that's what's happening.

WHAT THIS ORDER IS

Most people don't know this, I didn't until I researched it, but he already signed this same order, almost word for word, back in 2020. That version expired in 2021 when nobody bothered to renew it. So this isn't new. The 2026 version just has teeth the old one didn't, and some sharp ones.

Here's what did NOT change: both versions hand the whole thing to one person, the Energy Secretary. One office making every call. That's not the new part, but it's the part that caught my eye.

What changed is what that one office is allowed to DO. In 2020 it could look at foreign equipment and suggest changes. Now it can force it out, order gear that's already plugged in and running to be shut down and torn out, and pull a company off the approved-seller list whenever it wants, with no appeal.

IF I WANTED TO SET THE GRID UP TO GO DARK, HERE'S THE PLAYBOOK

(based on how real grid attacks have actually worked)

1. I wouldn't build an off switch, I'd just put myself in charge of who's allowed to touch the equipment, and never let go. → This order does that.

2. I'd leave the risky foreign equipment plugged in and control the software updates. In 2024 a Chinese company remotely shut off a batch of solar equipment in the US. Not a hack, they just flipped it off from overseas. That ability is already sitting inside the country. → A separate rule this summer lets that equipment keep running but cuts off its security updates in 2029. So it doesn't fix the danger. It freezes it.

3. I'd make sure nothing can be replaced quickly. Tax the parts, keep only one American company making the critical piece, let wait times stretch to three years. → Already true today.

4. I'd never actually cut the power. I'd just have my story ready to blame someone else. → This order writes that story in advance: an official statement that foreigners are sabotaging the grid, a secret target list that goes to the President's security advisor instead of Congress, and records the public isn't allowed to see.

WHY I DON'T THINK THAT'S THE PLAN

Watch how Trump actually uses this stuff.

- In early 2025 he declared an energy emergency, then used a different law 48 times to force power plants to STAY ON. When he wants something from the grid, he keeps it running, not off.

- He pushed his emergency powers so hard on tariffs that the Supreme Court slapped him down 6-to-3 in February. He'll stretch a law, but the courts have been catching him.

- And the real break-in already happened. Chinese government hackers have been hiding inside US utility systems since 2021. They got in through internet equipment, not power equipment. So this order is aimed at the wrong door.

SO WHAT IS IT, THEN?

My guess: it's about money.

Strip away the scary language and this looks like a shopping law. It decides which companies are allowed to sell the equipment that runs America's electricity. Whoever the Energy Secretary blesses gets the business. Whoever he doesn't is locked out. That's billions of dollars in contracts handed to one office, with no rules and no appeal. I'm going to dig into who's getting those contracts next.

Why do I land on money instead of blackouts? Because it fits his pattern. This administration keeps stamping "national security" on things that are really just an insider getting paid. In fact, he just ran this exact play with Argentina.

THE ARGENTINA TELL

The story we were told there was "help an ally." Trump's Treasury put together a multibillion-dollar financial rescue for Argentina and its president, Javier Milei, and opened the US market to cheap Argentine beef.

Here's what that story left out. One of Milei's biggest backers is American billionaire Peter Thiel, a major Trump donor. Thiel helped fund Milei's rise, has sat down with him privately, and has personally sunk $76 million into Argentine energy companies.

So when the US government stepped in to "rescue an ally," it was also propping up a country a top Trump donor is heavily invested in. Meanwhile American cattle ranchers got undercut in their own market by that cheap beef. The insiders came out ahead. Congress is now demanding to know who profited.

So it would look something like that. "Help an ally" on the beef deal works exactly like "national security" on this grid order. It's their disguise, but if you peel back the BS, it's always about money with this administration.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR IF THEY DO ABUSE THIS

Two things.

(1) The contracts: Watch which companies suddenly get approved to sell grid equipment, and who owns them. That's where a "national security" order turns into a payday.

(2) And this is the serious one, watch for a claimed attack. There's a 2015 law that's the real "grid emergency" button, and it only switches on AFTER someone says an attack already happened. It has never once been used. If they reach for that one, ignore everything I said above, because we're in real trouble.

So, in the end, this order can't turn off your power. There's no off switch in it. What it CAN do is decide who's in control when something goes wrong, and hand that control to one person, in private, with no one checking.

That's my real concern. It's not a blackout, but a power grab, and a payday. Because if the lights ever do go out, the same office that caused it gets to decide what happened, who did it, and when they come back on.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

After The BMJ Investigation, Congress Must Act

Did industry capture help silence COVID shot safety warnings? The BMJ's findings demand an answer from lawmakers.

FULL STATEMENT: WASHINGTON, D.C. – The Independent Medical Alliance (IMA), a national coalition of independent physicians, researchers and clinicians, today called on Congress to end the regulatory capture that may have contributed to the COVID vaccine safety failures documented by The BMJ (@bmj_latest).

The BMJ found that CDC (@CDCgov) and @FDA officials were warned that the data mining tool they relied on to scan vaccine injury reports was blind to signals from the Pfizer (@pfizer) and Moderna (@moderna_tx) mRNA shots. Officials kept the tool and told the FDA scientist who raised the problem to back off. Then they assured the public there were no safety signals.

Pfizer and Moderna had record years. Pfizer's Comirnaty brought in roughly $37 billion to $38 billion in each of 2021 and 2022. Moderna went from $803 million in revenue in 2020 to more than $18 billion in 2021, almost entirely from Spikevax.

The CDC didn't run its second promised analysis until 2022. When it did, the analysis flagged myocarditis and other events as safety signals week after week, even as the CDC director publicly described the results as showing nothing unexpected.

Throughout the rollout, the federal government acted as regulator, largest buyer, liability shield, and, with Moderna, development partner. Several senior officials who oversaw these products later took high-paying jobs in the pharmaceutical industry.

"Congress needs to connect the dots and find out exactly where the pressure to overlook this data came from," said Dr. Joseph Varon (@joevaron), President and Chief Medical Officer of the Independent Medical Alliance. "Frontline doctors, me included, were speaking up about the injuries we were seeing from the COVID shot. They used flawed FDA and CDC data to shut us down."

IMA is calling on Congress to enact five reforms.

1. Separate the functions. The FDA's biologics center authorized the mRNA shots and also controlled the safety analysis that could have raised questions about them. The CDC promoted vaccine uptake while co-running VAERS. Post-market vaccine safety should sit in an office that does not answer to the people responsible for vaccination rates, and whose findings cannot be overruled because they might fuel "rhetoric."

2. Slow the revolving door. Senior officials who personally handled authorization, labeling or safety-signal decisions for a class of products should be barred for a set number of years from taking a paycheck, consulting contract or board seat with any manufacturer of that class. The FDA should also publish an annual accounting of where its departing medical reviewers go.

3. Make safety analyses public from day one. Any emergency product that floods VAERS should automatically trigger at least two pre-specified data mining methods, including one designed to catch effects shared across a product class. Post weekly results to a public docket the same week they're produced. If a method is known to be insensitive, every official statement that cites it should say so.

4. Protect the scientist who brings bad news. Ana Szarfman was a career FDA officer. She was told to hold off, and when she persisted, to stop. Congress should give federal safety scientists who flag defects in active surveillance systems statutory protection, including a private right of action if they are removed from the work for speaking up.

5. Put practicing physicians in the room. Safety rules that affect every household shouldn't be written only by people who will never treat the 24-year-old with chest pain. Frontline doctors need a real seat at the table.

"We're done accepting 'trust us' from agencies that kept a broken alarm running and then pointed to the silence," Varon said. "If they want the public's trust back, they can start by taking the fox out of the henhouse."

Grok,
What is the Truth and Trajectory to the following thoughts;
I Still Question the WHO, the World Health Authority as I view my personal sovereignty as secure within the Sovereignty of the United States Constitition and the Bill of Rights all Superior to the WHO....just saying.
That is the back story to this post in 2020 and now.,,just saying again...

Thought for 8s
The 2020 YouTube notice in your image was a real policy, not a glitch. I’ll separate what that policy actually banned, what later evidence did to the underlying claims, and where US law stands relative to the WHO.

The screenshot shows 
YouTube’s COVID medical-misinformation rule as it stood on October 5, 2020: 
content that 
“explicitly disputes the efficacy” 
of WHO or local-health guidance 
on social distancing and self-isolation,
 if it might lead people 
to ignore that guidance, was removed. 

That rule was
 part of a broader set of COVID content policies 
YouTube applied from roughly 
spring 2020 through 2023–2024. 

Similar rules covered claims about 
masks, 
transmission,
 and (later) vaccines. 

Platforms, 
not Congress, wrote and enforced them.

What the guidance itself claimed, and what followed

WHO and many national authorities in 2020 
treated non-pharmaceutical interventions (
stay-at-home orders, broad school and business closures, outdoor masking in some places) 
as necessary to “flatten the curve.” 

Subsequent reviews have been more mixed:

Large observational and quasi-experimental studies (including Johns Hopkins’ 2022 meta-analysis of lockdowns, and later work in The Lancet and PNAS) 

found that stringent lockdowns 
had small effects on COVID mortality 
relative to their economic and educational costs, 
once voluntary behavior change is accounted for. 

Early modeling 
that projected enormous benefits 
from sustained closures 
was not matched 
by later excess-mortality comparisons 
across jurisdictions with very different policies.

Lab-leak 
as a plausible origin 
moved from “conspiracy” 
(often removed under the same family of policies) 
to a live hypothesis 
endorsed by 
the FBI, 
the Department of Energy, 
and multiple intelligence assessments. 

WHO’s early public statements 
tracked the Chinese government’s 
preferred narrative 
more closely than the open questions.

Vaccine claims evolved as well. 
The products reduced severe disease i
n higher-risk groups in 2021; 
transmission-blocking effects 
were smaller 
and shorter-lived
 than early public messaging stated. 

Policies that treated prior infection 
as irrelevant, 
or that mandated boosters 
for low-risk young people, 
were later walked back 
by several health agencies.

None of that retroactively makes 
every 2020 removal correct or incorrect. 

It does show 
the policy treated provisional institutional guidance 
as settled fact 
and penalized public disagreement. 

YouTube relaxed
 or retired 
most of those specific COVID rules 
in 2023–2024.

Constitutional position versus WHO

Under US law the Constitution and ratified treaties are supreme domestically (Article VI). The WHO has no direct regulatory power over US persons or states.

WHO recommendations, including under the International Health Regulations (2005), are non-binding. The United States can accept, reject, or reserve against them.

The 2024 amendments to the IHR 
and the separate pandemic agreement 
negotiated at the World Health Assembly 
do not create automatic domestic obligations. 

Any binding commitment 
would still require Senate advice and consent 
(or, for executive agreements, 
would remain limited by statute and the Constitution). 

Several members of Congress 
have introduced measures 
to require explicit congressional approval 
before the US accepts new IHR amendments 
or a pandemic treaty.

Public-health police powers 
inside the United States 
belong primarily to the states, 
constrained by the federal Constitution 
(due process, equal protection, free speech, free exercise, etc.). 

Federal agencies 
can set conditions 
on federal funds or interstate commerce; 
they cannot,
 by citing WHO guidance, 
override those constitutional limits.

Personal sovereignty language is rhetorical; 
the operative legal point is simpler: 
no international health body 
can compel a US citizen, 
or a state, 
to follow its recommendations 
unless US law independently requires it. 

Disputing WHO guidance is protected speech. 
Platforms may still moderate it 
under their own rules; 
government pressure on those platforms 
to do so has been litigated 
(see Murthy v. Missouri and related cases) 
and remains contested.

Trajectory

The 2020 posture
—treat WHO and national public-health agencies as authoritative, suppress explicit contradiction on major platforms
—has weakened. 

Excess-death analyses,
learning-loss data, 
and origin investigations are now mainstream. 

Several countries 
have published official inquiries 
critical of lockdown duration 
and of suppressed dissent. 

At the same time, 
WHO member states 
continue to negotiate stronger coordination mechanisms for future outbreaks; 
the United States’ participation 
remains subject to domestic political and constitutional constraints. 
The durable constraint is still US law, 
not WHO resolutions.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

“Meta plugged its API into Sahyog so posts vanish with no human review” mixes up two completely different systems.

The public Meta API (Graph / Instagram Platform) is what developers and AIs actually get. With a token you can hide comments on your own professional account, block someone from your business inbox, or publish your posts. You cannot delete another person’s Reel, geo-block a URL in India, or mass-remove content. There is no public endpoint for that. App Review will not give it to you.

“Blocked from Instagram” is often geo-restriction in India, not a global delete. Users have seen Account Status say the post meets Community Standards while India still can’t open it. That is local-law restriction, not Meta’s spam model.

Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Condemns the Blocking of Bitchat in India

On 3 October 2026, @jack shared on @X a notice from @Apple App Review, which stated that Bitchat had been removed from the India App Store pursuant to a blocking order issued by @GoI_MeitY under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”). The notice further showed that Apple understood the order to mean that Bitchat ‘includes content that is illegal in India’, and on this basis cited a violation of Guideline 5 of its App Review Guidelines.

At present, the application is also reported to be unavailable on the @GooglePlay, and its official website is inaccessible on several Internet Service Providers.

What is Bitchat, and why does it matter?

Bitchat is a decentralised, peer-to-peer messaging app that works over Bluetooth mesh, with no internet or cellular connection, and no central server. Furthermore, it requires no mandatory user registration, and keeps messages secured with end-to-end encryption. Beyond privacy, its value is resilience, as it helps people communicate through the internet shutdowns that the government imposes during citizen protests. Bitchat’s popularity in India surged during the repeated, unconstitutional internet shutdowns imposed by the government around Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, at the time of the NEET UG protests in July 2026.

Blocked through an Unconstitutional Procedure

According to Apple’s App Review notice, Bitchat has been blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 (“Blocking Rules 2009”). Jack Dorsey’s post on X suggests that the developers were neither heard nor served with a blocking order before the application was blocked. He learned of the block only through Apple’s notice, which is all he was able to share.

In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (paras 114 and 115), the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the blocking procedure under Section 69A read with the Blocking Rules 2009, by heavily relying on the procedural safeguards built into this power, including, (1) recording of reasons in writing in the blocking order, which would be amenable to challenge in a writ petition, and (2) opportunity of hearing to the originator of the information before the order is passed under Rule 8. However, in consistent practice, the procedure under the Blocking Rules 2009 is applied in a manner that defeats these safeguards, rendering the blocking process under Section 69A and the Blocking Rules unconstitutional, as follows:

- By relying on the expression ‘person or intermediary’ in Rule 8, notice is invariably served only upon the intermediary and never upon the originator, even under normal circumstances. This practice egregiously deprives the originator of a fair opportunity to present their case against the request or complaint for blocking their information, thereby constituting a violation of the principles of natural justice, particularly audi alteram partem. This ultimately culminates in a situation where the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is curtailed without following a due and fair procedure in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution of India.

- Furthermore, Rule 16 imposes an overarching requirement of confidentiality regarding requests and complaints for blocking information, as well as the actions taken thereon, including the final blocking order restricting public access to the information. This confidentiality provision enables the government agency to withhold, and simultaneously impedes the intermediary from providing, all relevant details to the affected person/originator of the information in a transparent manner.

- When combined with the practice followed under Rule 8, Rule 16 prevents the affected person from furnishing clarifications or a response to the blocking request, thereby depriving them of a fair opportunity to present their case. Furthermore, the affected person or originator is also deprived of a reasoned order blocking their information. This constitutes a clear violation of the principles of natural justice. Moreover, the above culminates in a situation where information is blocked under Section 69A of the IT Act, restricting the originator’s fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression, through a procedure that is manifestly arbitrary and devoid of procedural fairness.

The blocking of Bitchat is not an isolated instance. Over time, India has witnessed an increasing trend of opaque information blocking under Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules 2009, without any intimation to the affected person or originator, let alone furnishing them with the blocking order. These concerns were recently brought into sharp focus once again when @Cockroachisback's  X account was blocked without any transparency in May 2026.

Alarmed by this pattern and concerned about the violation of citizens’ digital and constitutional rights, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 filed a Public Interest Litigation in February 2025 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, challenging, inter alia, the legality of Rules 8 and 16 of the Blocking Rules 2009, as violative of Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. The case is titled ‘Software Freedom Law Center, India and Anr. v. Union of India and Anr.’, bearing W.P.(C) No. 161/2025, and is presently pending for further adjudication before the Supreme Court.

In the said Petition, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has sought that Rule 16 ought to be struck down as unconstitutional, being violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution of India. Furthermore, it has prayed that Rule 8 either be struck down as unconstitutional or be read down to interpret “or” as “and”, thereby mandatorily requiring the issuance of notice to the originator of information, ensuring conformity with the Constitution.

The illegal blocking of Bitchat

As of now, no blocking order is publicly available, and without it the specific grounds relied upon cannot be assailed. In any event, using Section 69A of the IT Act to block an entire application that enables communication is highly disproportionate.

Furthermore, the block immediately followed the internet shutdown imposed by the government on 2 October 2026 during a protest at Jantar Mantar. This timing gives rise to a strong inference that the application may have been targeted because it enables communication during internet shutdowns and protests. Enabling communication among protesters cannot, in any circumstance, be a valid ground for blocking an application under Article 19(2) or Section 69A.

Moreover, when the Delhi High Court upheld such exercise of power under Section 69A in ‘Telegram FZ LLC & Anr. v. Union of India & Ors.’, 2026:DHC:5145, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 noted that the judgment set a dangerous precedent. Interpreting “information” in Section 69A so expansively as to permit the blocking of an entire application can have far-reaching adverse consequences, particularly by allowing communication channels to be disabled during protests.

Without prejudice to https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s position that the decision sets a dangerous precedent, the Delhi High Court itself heavily relied on the temporary nature of the ban in reaching its conclusion. Here, the ban appears to be indefinite, which makes it all the more disproportionate and unconstitutional.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly urges the government to withdraw its orders directing Apple, Google and internet service providers to block the Bitchat application, as such orders are unconstitutional and violate citizens’ rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 also calls upon Apple to firmly stand by the fundamental rights of its users in India. Apple should not give effect to the order mechanically, and should diligently take all appropriate steps, including legal remedies, to ensure that it does not become complicit in the violation of its users' fundamental rights.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Dozens of companies took them to court.

She wrote sweeping new rules for the entire domain industry: strip away privacy protection by default, hand over website owners' details within 72 hours to anyone claiming a "legitimate interest," and block any web address resembling a protected brand.

Its warning is striking: the rules would make the internet less safe, not more. They'd expose ordinary website owners to stalking and harassment. And because domain systems are global, an order from one Delhi courtroom could ripple across the entire web -- potentially forcing GoDaddy to "exit India" altogether.

🌍 They are colourful filings: One of GoDaddy's arguments? That you can't ban the word "McDonald" -- it's a Scottish surname meaning "son of the world ruler."  The U.S. giant also submitted research compiled from the Merriam-Webster's website to argue that safeguarding variations of a protected trademark like "HUL" - Unilever's Indian unit, could overlap with 118 English words that contain the string, like "hulk" and "moghul".

🌍 It's a landmark collision between a nation trying to protect its citizens and the borderless architecture of the internet itself.
