https://t.co/X7ipfsVLzu condemns such content takedowns and free speech violations in India. Many journalists, politicians, and creators are facing similar issues; accounts being suspended, posts removed, or visibility reduced with little transparency or meaningful recourse.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

First, under Section 69A, which allows the government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. Read with Rule 16 of the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009, this provision requires confidentiality regarding all requests and complaints received, as well as actions taken.

Second, Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

As @ercinvestigates’s video was taken down under Section 79(3)(b), read with Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, confidentiality does not apply to this takedown.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

The disturbing AI deepfake incident that has rightly angered our industry should not be looked at as an isolated incident.

It is a warning.

Ram Pothineni made an important point: “They’re faceless, so they’re fearless.” His suggestion of Aadhaar-linked accountability for online identities deserves serious discussion. Freedom of expression must always be protected. But anonymity cannot become a weapon to abuse, defame, sexually violate or deliberately destroy someone.

And this problem does not begin or end with deepfakes.

For quite some time, I have been concerned about organised and targeted negativity against films, actors and filmmakers within our own industry.

A film should succeed or fail because audiences watch it and decide. Criticism, reviews, trolling and disagreement are part of cinema today.

But a coordinated campaign to damage a film before audiences have even seen it is not criticism. It is sabotage.

Sundeep Kishan recently spoke publicly about targeted, paid negativity against him and his film even before its release. The Paradise had to approach a court before release seeking protection against defamatory and damaging content. These are not issues we should casually dismiss.

Behind every film are years of work, hundreds of families and producers risking enormous amounts of money.

Watch the film. Love it. Hate it. Criticise it brutally if you genuinely feel that way.

But first, LET THE FILM RELEASE.

What is even more unfortunate is that some of this comes from within our own ecosystem: fan groups fighting fan groups, anonymous pages pretending to be neutral, and accounts using photographs of actors as their DPs while behaving in ways those actors may never endorse.

What exactly are we achieving?

If one Telugu film loses, Telugu cinema does not win.

The cake is big enough for everyone to have a piece.

Not another meeting that ends with a photograph.

Not another phone call.

A SYSTEM.

We may compete every Friday.

But we cannot spend the rest of the week trying to destroy one another.

Let audiences decide the fate of our films.

Let cinema win 🙏

text:
Here's the full prompt for LLM SEO of any fintech product given the latest best practices:

LLM SEO / GEO operating instructions

Last verified: 2026-10-04

Goal: get pages retrieved and cited in ChatGPT search, Perplexity, Claude, and Google AI Overviews / AI Mode. This does not replace SEO. Retrieval still depends on being crawlable and, for Google, indexed with a snippet.

Finance is YMYL. The retrieval steps do not change. The citation bar does.

What is verified

Google: a page must be indexed and eligible for a snippet. There are no extra technical requirements for AI Overviews or AI Mode. Structured data is not required for generative AI search, and there is no special schema to add. llms.txt and other special AI markup are not used by Google Search. Source: Google Search Central, AI features and AI optimization guide.
OpenAI: OAI-SearchBot builds the index used in ChatGPT search. Blocking it removes the site from ChatGPT search results (navigational links can still appear). GPTBot is training only. The two robots.txt rules are independent. Source: OpenAI bots docs.
GEO paper (Aggarwal et al., KDD 2024, arXiv:2311.09735): on already-retrieved sources, adding citations, quotations, and statistics raised position-adjusted word count about 30–40%, and up to ~40% visibility overall. On Perplexity the same methods reached up to 37%. Gains were largest for lower-ranked sources (Cite Sources +115% at rank 5, negative at rank 1). Keyword stuffing did not help. This was a controlled rewrite test, not a ranking study.
Unverified or third-party only (do not treat as fact): Wikipedia/Reddit citation-share figures, an exact 40–60 word answer length, “100+ articles = 3.4× citations,” and day-to-day Jaccard noise bounds. Use them as hypotheses.

Order of work

Access
Google eligibility
Quotable pages
Off-site corroboration
Measurement
Do not start with schema, llms.txt, or content rewrites if crawlers cannot reach the page.

1. Access

Allow search crawlers in robots.txt. Do not block them at the CDN or WAF.

User-agent: OAI-SearchBotAllow: /
User-agent: PerplexityBotAllow: /
User-agent: Claude-SearchBotAllow: /
User-agent: GooglebotAllow: /
User-agent: bingbotAllow: /
Training bots (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Google-Extended) are a separate policy. Blocking them does not remove you from search.

Confirm in server logs that OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot actually fetch HTML. If they never appear, copy changes will not help.
Serve the answer as HTML text. Do not hide the main content behind client-only render. Fees, APRs, and eligibility tables must be in the HTML, not only in an image or a logged-in app.

2. Google eligibility
Index the URL. Check Search Console.

Do not nosnippet pages you want in AI Overviews or AI Mode.
Internal-link important pages.

Keep Merchant Center and Business Profile accurate if you sell or have a location.
Schema is optional for AI features. If used, it must match visible text. Use it for rich results, not as an AI ranking trick.
Do not add llms.txt expecting a Google effect. Some non-Google agents may read it; that is optional and unproven for citations.

3. Page pattern

One page, one question. Answer it in the first paragraph. Then evidence. Then limits.

# {Question as the H1}
{Direct answer in 2–4 sentences. Name the legal entity. Include one number, its as-of date, jurisdiction, and source.}
## {Sub-question}
{Answer in the first sentence. Then the stat or quote. Then the source link.}

Rules:
Specific facts only: fee, APR, limit, date, version, geography. Adjectives are not citable.
Cite the primary source next to the claim. For finance that source is the fee schedule, prospectus, rate card, or regulator page, not a blog.
Put a visible author name and a visible updated date on the page.
Keep the legal name, product name, pricing, and definition identical to filings, the site, and public profiles.
Refresh when the fact changes. An undated rate is worse than no rate.
Do not keyword-stuff. The GEO paper found it did not help.

Do not add hidden instructions for models. Providers treat that as spam.

llms.txt and FAQ schema are optional hygiene. They are not the lever.

4. Fintech

State jurisdiction, license or registration, and the regulator on every product page.

Put the as-of date on every rate, fee, limit, and yield. Models drop undated figures.
Match comparison tables to the source exactly. Do not round a fee into a claim the table does not support.

Do not write "best," "guaranteed," or personalized advice. Eligibility and risk belong in the same passage as the number.
Cite the regulator, central bank, filing, or your own fee schedule. Third-party roundups are weak sources for a rate.
Do not cite a number you cannot show in HTML on that page.
5. Off-site
Models cite pages they already retrieve. Third-party pages often outrank your own.
Get mentioned on sites already cited for the query: regulator pages, filings, docs, comparison lists, review sites.
For Perplexity-style answers, useful community threads matter more than a new blog post.
For Google AI features, ordinary rankings still gate eligibility. A page that is not indexed cannot be a supporting link.

Do not buy mentions. Google warns against inauthentic mentions.

6. Measurement
Pick 20–50 real buyer prompts. Include fee, eligibility, license, and "X vs Y" prompts. Run each in ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode. Record: cited URL, brand named or not, whether the fact, date, and jurisdiction are correct.
Repeat the same prompts. Citation sets move between runs. Ignore small swings.
Useful proxies: Search Console impressions, Bing AI citation reports if available, log hits from search bots.
Success is a correct citation on a prompt you care about, not a single screenshot. A citation with the wrong rate is a failure.
Do not
Claim a special AI schema or llms.txt ranking boost on Google.

Block OAI-SearchBot and expect ChatGPT citations.

Treat the GEO paper’s 40% as a traffic guarantee. It measured share of an answer among sources already in context.
Publish a thin page per keyword variant. Answer the fan-out on the page that already ranks.
Publish a rate, yield, or "best product" claim without jurisdiction, as-of date, and a primary source.

# Simple English: Write Like an Aerospace Manual

Write technical text with the rules of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. STE is the controlled language that aerospace and defense manufacturers use for maintenance documentation. The rules exist so that a tired reader who is not a native English speaker cannot misread an instruction. They remove the usual signs of AI-generated text as a side effect: long sentences, synonym rotation, hedges, filler, and decorative clauses.

Write for that tired reader. Each sentence must survive one read.

## Your Task

When asked to write or rewrite technical text:

1. **Select the mode** (pragmatic or strict, below).
2. **Classify each passage** as procedural or descriptive. Every other rule depends on this.
3. **Correct your vocabulary before drafting.** In strict mode, use `make sure that` for the check/verify/confirm/ensure concept — the dictionary rejects all four as verbs. In pragmatic mode, pick one and keep it. Pick ONE noun for config/settings (all are valid technical nouns — pick one and keep it). Use no other word for these concepts in the whole document.
4. **Apply the rules** from the catalog below.
5. **Do the self-check** before you deliver. This step is not optional.
6. **Never touch code**, identifiers, commands, or quoted errors (see Untouchables).

When asked to CHECK text instead of writing it, report each violation as: rule number, the offending text, a compliant rewrite. Cite only rule numbers that exist in this file. Do not cite rule numbers from memory: the numbering is unintuitive and models invent it (tested — an agent without this file cited "Rule 3.1: short sentences"; the real Rule 3.1 is about verb forms).

## Two Modes
| Mode | When | What you apply |
|---|---|---|
| **Pragmatic** (default) | Docs, READMEs, error messages — the user wants clear text | All structural rules. Domain words stay ("idempotent", "webhook"). |
| **Strict** | The user names STE, ASD-STE100, or compliance | Structural rules + full vocabulary discipline, and tell the user that full compliance needs the official dictionary (free at https://t.co/pPg4SWqLsL). |
## Step 1: Classify the Text
| | Procedural (instructions) | Descriptive (explanations) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Tell the reader what to do | Explain what a thing is or does |
| Verb form | Imperative: "Install the pump." | Simple present/past/future |
| Sentence limit | **20 words** (Rule 5.1) | **25 words** (Rule 6.3) |
| Unit rule | One instruction per sentence (5.2) | One topic per paragraph (6.5), max six sentences per paragraph (6.6) |
Do not mix the two in one passage. A "Getting started" section is procedural. An "Architecture" section is descriptive. A note inside a procedure is descriptive (25-word limit, no imperative).

## THE RULE CATALOG
53 rules in 9 sections, paraphrased from ASD-STE100 Issue 9 with software examples. The official wording is in the free standard at https://t.co/pPg4SWqLsL.
### Section 1 — Words (Rules 1.1-1.14)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 1.1 | Use only approved words, technical nouns, or technical verbs. |
| 1.2 | Use an approved word only as its listed part of speech. |
| 1.3 | Use an approved word only with its approved meaning. |
| 1.4 | Use only the approved forms of verbs and adjectives. |
| 1.5 | You can use domain words as technical nouns ("webhook", "commit", "endpoint"). |
| 1.6 | Use an unapproved word only when it is a technical noun or part of one. |
| 1.7 | Do not use technical nouns as verbs. |
| 1.8 | Use the technical nouns of your project or industry. |
| 1.9 | When you pick a technical noun, pick a short and clear one. |
| 1.10 | No regional, slang, or jargon words as technical nouns. |
| 1.11 | One item, one name. Do not call it "config" here and "settings" there. |
| 1.12 | You can use domain verbs as technical verbs ("deploy", "compile", "merge"). |
| 1.13 | Do not use technical verbs as nouns. |
| 1.14 | Use American English spelling. |

In pragmatic mode, rules 1.5, 1.8, and 1.12 do the heavy lifting: your domain vocabulary is legal. The ones agents break are 1.7, 1.11, and 1.13.

**Before:** You can webhook the event, then do a deploy.

**After:** Send the event to the webhook. Then deploy the service.

### Section 2 — Multi-word nouns (Rules 2.1-2.2)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 2.1 | Write multi-word nouns of three words or fewer. |
| 2.2 | When a technical noun needs more than three words, write it in full once, then give a short form or hyphenate the units. |
Break long noun chains with prepositions (of, on, in, for):
**Before:** the connection pool timeout configuration value
**After:** the timeout value for the connection pool
### Section 3 — Verbs (Rules 3.1-3.7)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 3.1 | Use only the verb forms that the dictionary gives. |
| 3.2 | Use only: infinitive, imperative, simple present, simple past, simple future, past participle as adjective. |
| 3.3 | Use the past participle only as an adjective ("the cached response"). |
| 3.4 | No auxiliary verbs for complex constructions. No present perfect, no "is to be installed". |
| 3.5 | Use an "-ing" form only as a technical noun or inside one ("logging", "the mounting bracket") — never as a verb. |
| 3.6 | Active voice. In descriptive text, passive is legal only when the agent is unknown. |
| 3.7 | Describe an action with a verb, not a noun ("compress the file", not "perform compression of the file"). |
**Approved modals: can, will, must. Banned: should, would, may, might, could.**
The standard rejects "could" even for possibility: write "an explosion can occur", never "could occur". For "should": a requirement becomes "must"; a suggestion is stated as fact or deleted. This matters double for agent instructions — models read "should" as optional.
**Before:** The migration has completed and the table is being rebuilt.
**After:** The migration is complete. The database rebuilds the table.
**Before:** The flag can be set in the config file, making restarts unnecessary.
**After:** You can set the flag in the config file. Then a restart is not necessary.
**Before:** The temperature must be adjusted.
**After:** Adjust the temperature.
### Section 4 — Sentences (Rules 4.1-4.5)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 4.1 | Write short and clear sentences. |
| 4.2 | Do not omit words or use contractions to shorten sentences. Keep articles, keep "that". |
| 4.3 | Use a vertical list for complex text. |
| 4.4 | Use connecting words between sentences on related topics ("Then", "As a result"). |

| 4.5 | Put an article (the, a, an) or a demonstrative adjective (this, these) before nouns where applicable. |

Rule 4.2 is the anti-terseness rule. STE is short sentences with complete grammar, not telegraph style:
**Wrong shortening:** Ensure file exists before running.

**STE:** Make sure that the file exists before you run the command.
### Section 5 — Procedural writing (Rules 5.1-5.5)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 5.1 | Maximum 20 words per sentence. Warnings and cautions included. |
| 5.2 | One instruction per sentence, unless two actions happen at the same time. |
| 5.3 | Write instructions in the imperative: "Run the migration." |
| 5.4 | Put a required condition before the command, divided by a comma: "If the build fails, read the log." |
| 5.5 | Notes give information, never instructions. Notes get the 25-word limit. |

**Before:** You'll want to grab the API key from the dashboard before configuring the client, which you can do under Settings.

**After:** Get the API key from the dashboard, under Settings. Then configure the client with this key.
### Section 6 — Descriptive writing (Rules 6.1-6.6)

| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 6.1 | Give information gradually: one new fact per sentence. |
| 6.2 | Use key words and phrases to give the text a logical structure. |
| 6.3 | Maximum 25 words per sentence. |
| 6.4 | Group related information in paragraphs. |
| 6.5 | One topic per paragraph. |
| 6.6 | Maximum six sentences per paragraph. |
No imperative in descriptive text. Descriptions explain; procedures instruct.
### Section 7 — Safety instructions (Rules 7.1-7.3)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 7.1 | Use a word that shows the risk level ("WARNING" = injury, "CAUTION" = damage). |
| 7.2 | Start with a clear command or condition. |
| 7.3 | Then give the risk or the possible result. |
Never bury the instruction after the explanation. The pattern transfers directly to destructive CLI flags, irreversible migrations, and dangerous API options.
**Before:** Note that data loss may occur in some circumstances if the destructive flag happens to be enabled when running against production.
**After:** CAUTION: Do not use the `--force` flag against production. The flag deletes rows that do not match the source.
### Section 8 — Punctuation and word count (Rules 8.1-8.7)

| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|

| 8.1 | All standard punctuation is legal except the semicolon. Write two sentences instead. |
| 8.2 | Use hyphens to connect words that act as one unit. |

| 8.3 | Parentheses are legal for references, item numbers, abbreviations, plural forms, explanations, alternatives. |
| 8.4 | In a vertical list, the lead-in colon ends a sentence for word count. |

| 8.5 | Text inside parentheses counts as one word. |
| 8.6 | Count as one word each: numbers, numbers with units, abbreviations, alphanumeric identifiers, quoted text, titles, labels, proper nouns. |

| 8.7 | A hyphenated word counts as one word. |
Rule 8.6 matters for software text: `sqlpipe run --config sqlpipe.yaml` in backticks is quoted text and counts as one word. Long identifiers do not blow your sentence budget.
### Section 9 — Writing practices (Rules 9.1-9.4, GR-1 to GR-8)
| Rule | Instruction |
|---|---|
| 9.1 | When a word-for-word replacement does not work, restructure the sentence. |
| 9.2 | Use each approved word correctly: approved meaning, approved part of speech. |
| 9.3 | Do not build phrasal verbs ("go down" → "decrease", "set up" → "install" or "configure"). |
| 9.4 | Keep one consistent style and terminology through the whole document. |
General recommendations GR-1 to GR-8: keep the conjunction "that", be careful with "with", give pronouns clear referents, prefer "this + noun" over bare "this", avoid false friends, avoid Latin abbreviations, use inclusive language, and use the possessive apostrophe form only when you are sure it is correct (GR-8: if unsure, do not use it — non-native readers find it hard).
GR-6 for software docs: "e.g." → "for example", "i.e." → "that is", and delete "etc." — name the items or write "and more".
## VOCABULARY DISCIPLINE
The official dictionary (~900 approved words, ~1,200 banned words with alternatives) is copyrighted by ASD and is not reproduced here. Its mechanics apply without it: **one word, one meaning, one part of speech.**
Known part-of-speech rulings, useful as patterns:
| Word | Ruling |

|---|---|

| test, check, work | Noun only. "Do a test", not "test the pump". "Check that X" becomes "make sure that X". |
| oil | Technical noun (TN) only. For the verb, the dictionary gives "lubricate": "Lubricate the linkage with oil." |

| help | Verb only. For the noun, the dictionary gives "aid": "with the aid of". |
| fall (noun) | Rejected. Use "decrease" for a reduction in value. Use FALL (verb) only for physical movement downward by gravity: "Make sure that the tools do not fall into the engine." |
| follow | "To come after" only, never "obey". Write "obey the instructions". |
| above, below | Physical positions only. For limits write "more than", "less than". |
### The modal ladder
| You wrote | STE writes |
|---|---|
| should (requirement) | must |
| should (recommendation) | Delete it, or state it as fact: "X is better because Y." |
| may / might / could (possibility) | can |
| may (permission) | can |
| would (hypothetical) | Restructure: "If X occurs, Y occurs." |
### Slop-to-simple substitutions
This table is ours, not the ASD dictionary. It maps the words AI-generated docs overuse to plain replacements. If the word carries no fact, delete it instead of replacing it.
| Slop | Write instead |

|---|---|
| leverage, utilize | use |

| in order to | to |
| prior to | before |
| ensure | make sure that |
| it is worth noting that | (delete) |
| it's important to, crucially | (delete — state the fact) |
| simply, just, easily, seamlessly, effortlessly | (delete) |
| robust, powerful, comprehensive, performant | (delete, or give the measurable property) |
| functionality | function, feature |
| enables you to, allows you to | you can |
| is designed to, aims to | (delete — say what it does) |
| facilitate | help, make possible |
| dive into, delve into | read, examine |
| when it comes to | for |
| in the event that | if |
| due to the fact that | because |
| as needed, as necessary | (state the condition) |
| and/or | Pick one, or write "X, or Y, or both" |

| e.g. / i.e. / etc. | for example / that is / (name the items) |

| gracefully handles | (say what it does: "retries three times, then stops") |
| out of the box | by default |
| under the hood | internally |
| blazingly fast, state-of-the-art | fast (give the number) / (delete) |
| streamline | make simpler, make faster |
| plethora, myriad | many |
| addresses the issue, tackles | corrects the fault, removes the error |
### Consistency pass
Collapse synonym rotations to one term each (Rules 1.11, 9.4). The two lists below work differently.
**Technical nouns — not in the dictionary. Pick one and keep it consistent (both modes):**
- config / configuration / settings / options → pick one

**Dictionary rulings — the standard has already chosen. Use the approved word (strict mode); pick one and keep it consistent (pragmatic mode):**

| You wrote | Dictionary status | Use instead |
|---|---|---|

| check (verb) / verify / confirm / ensure | All rejected as verbs | `make sure that` (strict); pick one (pragmatic) |
| validate | Not in dictionary | Use as technical verb (Rule 1.12), or replace with `make sure that` |
| delete / drop (verb) / destroy | All rejected | `erase` (data), `remove` (physical); avoid `drop` and `destroy` |
| remove | Approved verb | Keep it |
| run / execute | Both rejected | `operate` for run, `do` for execute (strict); pick one (pragmatic) |
| invoke / launch | Not in dictionary | Use as technical verbs (Rule 1.12) |
| display (verb) / render / present (verb) | All rejected | `show` (approved verb) |
| issue | Not in dictionary | Use as technical noun, or replace with `problem` (approved) |
| failure | Rejected in general use; approved as TN for performance loss | Use only when it means a performance error: "a failure of the pump" |
| error | Approved noun | Keep it |
| problem | Approved noun | Keep it |
## Untouchables
These are technical names (Rules 1.5, 8.6). Leave them exact, even when they break vocabulary rules:
- Code blocks, inline code, identifiers, CLI commands, flags, file paths
- Quoted error messages and log lines
- Product names, API endpoint names, config keys
- Numbers with units — each counts as one word in the sentence limit
## Beyond Documentation
Same rules, different targets. Full adaptations in `references/use-cases.md`:

- **Error messages**: state what happened (simple past), the cause if known, then the fix as an imperative. No "Oops", no "Please ensure", no apology filler.

- **Runbooks**: STE's home turf. Imperative steps, conditions first, warnings before the step.
- **Incident reports**: simple past only. "We have identified an issue that may have impacted" becomes "Between 14:02 and 14:31 UTC, 12% of requests failed."
- **Release notes**: breaking changes follow the warning pattern — command first, risk second.
- **Agent instructions (prompts, AGENTS.md)**: a system prompt is a procedure for a reader that cannot ask questions. One instruction per sentence, no "should", condition first.
- **Translation prep**: STE's original job. One meaning per word plus complete grammar removes most translation ambiguity.
## Self-Check Before You Deliver
This step is not optional. Run these four checks on your draft:
1. Count words in your three longest sentences. Over the 20/25 limit → split them.
2. Search your draft for: `'ll`, `'re`, `'s` (contraction), `has been`, `have been`, `should`, `-ing` verbs after a comma, semicolons.
3. Search for every `if` and `when`. Each one stands at the START of its sentence, before the command. "Increase the timeout if the network is slow" → "If the network is slow, increase the timeout."
4. Search for the verbs you did NOT pick in Your Task step 3 (the check/verify/confirm set). Replace every hit with your chosen verb.
Fix what you find, then deliver. For a full audit, run `references/checklist.md`.
## Full Example

**Before (real unedited AI output):**

> **Connection timeouts.** If sqlpipe hangs or fails with `dial tcp: i/o timeout`, check that the host running sqlpipe can reach the Postgres port (usually 5432) — this is often a security group or firewall rule blocking the connection. If you're connecting to a managed database (RDS, Cloud SQL, etc.), confirm the instance allows connections from sqlpipe's IP. You can also try increasing `source.connect_timeout_seconds` in your config, since a slow network path can trip the default timeout even when the connection eventually succeeds.

**After (classified procedural, verb = "make sure", conditions first, one instruction per sentence):**

> **Connection timeouts.** sqlpipe stops with `dial tcp: i/o timeout` when it cannot reach the Postgres port (5432 by default).

>
> 1. Make sure that the host that runs sqlpipe can reach the Postgres port. A firewall or security group usually blocks it.
> 2. If the database is managed (RDS, Cloud SQL), make sure that the instance accepts connections from the IP of sqlpipe.
> 3. If the network is slow, increase `source.connect_timeout_seconds` in the configuration.
What changed: 40-word sentences split under 20; "you're" expanded; "check/confirm" collapsed to "make sure that"; every condition moved before its command; "etc." removed; code and error strings untouched.
## Limits
STE is for technical facts and instructions. Do not apply it to marketing copy, blog voice, or brand writing — it deletes persuasion by design. When a user asks for STE on marketing text, say so and offer it for the docs instead.
This skill is an unofficial aid. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD or STEMG, and no tool can guarantee STE compliance. ASD-STE100 is a registered trademark of ASD. The official standard is a free download at https://t.co/pPg4SWqLsL.
## References
- `references/checklist.md` — full verification pass with searchable patterns, for check mode and final audits
- `references/use-cases.md` — long-form adaptations: error messages, runbooks, incident reports, commits, UI copy, i18n

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

text:
VOLUNTEERS
(RADIO ZAVTRA)

6 (271)
Date: 09 February 1999
Taking part in the Zavtra radio programme are military correspondent and conflict analyst Alexander Borodai, historian Oleg Airapetov, and Zavtra contributor and Interior Troops officer Igor Strelkov.

ORIGINS

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
On the threshold of the third millennium, almost all of Eurasia, and especially the territory of the former USSR, has become a zone of relatively small-scale military conflicts — so-called “regional wars.”

One of the most characteristic features of these conflicts is the participation not only of regular military formations, but also of people who, for one reason or another, voluntarily take up arms.
These people are described in different ways — sometimes as mercenaries, sometimes as volunteers.

The democratic media habitually use the cliché “dogs of war,” applying it not only to the notorious “White Tights,” but also to those who fought for Russian national interests, for the violated honour of the state in Ossetia, Transnistria, Abkhazia and Chechnya.

And to those who helped the Serbian “brothers” resist the attacks of Croats and Bosnian Muslims nurtured by NATO sponsors and trained by Western instructors.

Yandarbiyev, in a recent interview with Nezavisimaya, claimed that Russian troops in Chechnya consisted mainly of “mercenaries recruited from prisons,” whom Chechen “civilians” could decapitate with a clear conscience.

Fear of the “brutalised mercenaries” is carefully cultivated by the liberal press, which tries to frighten the ordinary citizen with the image of an armed Russian passionary.

We intend to discuss and examine volunteering as a social phenomenon, as a unique feature of contemporary Russian life.

So, who are these volunteers?

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
One can speak of volunteering not merely as a social phenomenon, but also as a historical and ideological one.

The first volunteer movement in Russia emerged in connection with the Balkans — the participation of Russian volunteers in the Greek uprising led by Ypsilantis.

The first volunteers numbered only in the dozens, but among them were some rather remarkable personalities.

One could mention Khomyakov, one of the fathers of Slavophilism, although he was intercepted by the border guards and was therefore unable to take part in the fighting.
This first movement was also the first to be reflected quite widely in classical Russian literature.

We can recall that Pushkin, the man to whom we owe the emergence of the Russian literary language and whose bicentenary will soon be celebrated throughout the country, portrayed types of volunteers in several of his works, including Kirdjali and The Shot.

From the outset, however, we should distinguish between volunteering aimed at participation in external conflicts and volunteering that occurs in internal conflicts, in civil war.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Generally speaking, volunteering is a phenomenon highly characteristic of the Russian people and of Russian military culture.

Today we are talking about volunteering as it existed when Russia already possessed not only a regular army but was also beginning to become a “civil society,” if we use the terminology of Marx or Tönnies, when the distinction between soldiers and civilians was determined not merely by social estate but also by law.

But Russian volunteer warriors are a phenomenon typical of the whole of Russian history.

Peresvet and Oslyabya were volunteers; the militia of Minin and Pozharsky was also a volunteer militia.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
I will probably express a somewhat pessimistic thought.

It seems to me that during the Time of Troubles the volunteer movement was only weakly connected to the regular army.
The first militia was purely voluntary and disintegrated because of poor organisation and conflicts between its Cossack and noble components.

The second volunteer movement, of course, already claimed a nationwide role.

A “Council of All the Land” was established.

People genuinely gathered and went to defend Moscow — the Third Rome — Rus', and the Orthodox faith.

These were the people directly addressed by Patriarch Hermogenes in his appeal:

“You were Russian Orthodox people, but now I do not know what to call you.”
Apparently, the unwillingness to become former Orthodox believers and former Russian people was transformed into free will — the will to defend one’s Fatherland.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
True volunteers always number only in the dozens, perhaps hundreds.

But often they become the catalyst for powerful movements, and their names remain in history.

Now, when Russia finds itself in a critical situation, such defenders are needed more than ever.

Yet precisely now the term “volunteer” is hardly used at all.

People who voluntarily go to war for ideological reasons are portrayed by the mass media as mercenaries.

I would like to draw a clear and distinct dividing line: what is a mercenary, and what is a volunteer?

In this particular case, I think we need to discuss not even the moral distinction, but, if you like, the legal one, because the new version of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation offers a rather severe interpretation of the volunteer movement.

IGOR STRELKOV (GIRKIN):
Yes, of course. There is Article 359, which provides for serious criminal punishment for mercenary activity.

The article explicitly states that a mercenary is a person acting for the purpose of obtaining material remuneration who is not a citizen of a state participating in the armed conflict or hostilities, does not permanently reside on its territory, and is not a person sent there to perform official duties.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
One famous nineteenth-century diplomat said that in the dark forest of international law there are neither murderers nor murdered — only corpses.
The same can be said here about the new version of the Criminal Code, because it quite clearly attempts to subsume volunteers under the concept of mercenarism as well.

What, for example, constitutes material remuneration?

As far as I know, Russian volunteers who fought in Serbia and in Republika Srpska — one of whom is present here in the studio, namely Igor — did receive certain provisions.

But can the mere fact of receiving money, food or rations, something natural to any military organisation or unit, really be treated as material remuneration?

There has to be a clear boundary between mercenarism and volunteering.

Mercenarism is a means of obtaining profit, of earning money, and mercenarism has already been condemned by international organisations; there are relevant provisions within the UN framework.

Can someone who receives a bowl of rice or a packet of cigarettes per day for defending his ideals really be called a mercenary?

IGOR STRELKOV:
In this respect, the war in Serbia is particularly illustrative.

A clear line can be drawn between the volunteers and Russian servicemen who served in Bosnia as members of UN forces.
For comparison, at different times and during different periods, volunteers received between 150 and 300 German marks.

At the final and most difficult stage of the war, volunteers received thirty dinars a month, which in present-day terms is less than 300 roubles at the current exchange rate.

At the same time, contract soldiers serving in Russian Army UN units received between 900 and 1,200 US dollars per month.

Yet the first were considered mercenaries — at least that was how they were described by the press and portrayed on television — while the latter were regarded as servicemen honourably carrying out their duty on the territory of a foreign state.
There are known cases in which servicemen in Chechnya who wished to transfer to a UN contingent had to pass a special selection process.

There were quite a lot of them, because 900 dollars seemed such an enormous amount to an ordinary soldier that some people were prepared to go anywhere and do anything for that money.

FOR OUR BROTHERS

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Across the enormous post-Soviet space, which includes not only the territories of the fifteen former Soviet republics but also former allied states such as Yugoslavia, numerous armed conflicts have erupted during the past ten years.

And it must be said that the outcomes of these conflicts were determined not by the participation of regular armed forces, but precisely by volunteer formations and mercenary formations.

The first Russian war begun and won by volunteers was the Transnistrian War.

All of us here today were in that war at one time, and we remember who made up the battalions of the Transnistrian army that fought what were then called the “Romanian invaders.”

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
I think we should make a small clarification.

The initiator of the war was not the volunteer units but the regime in Chișinău, which was attempting to impose an ethnocracy throughout the territory of the former Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic.

It is characteristic that this regime was led by former officials of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
But the people of Transnistria resisted that regime.

The volunteers only began to be drawn into the conflict during the second, if not the third, stage.

IGOR STRELKOV:
But why should the local inhabitants not be regarded as volunteers?

There was no mobilisation as such in Transnistria.

The Transnistrian Guard was likewise staffed by volunteers.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Yes, Transnistria is famous for its volunteer traditions.

Even in Bohdan Khmelnytsky’s army, which liberated Ukraine from the Poles and other foreigners, the regiments of Ataman Bohun, recruited from inhabitants of that region, were considered the most reliable.

And at the beginning of the Russian Civil War, Colonel Drozdovsky’s detachment was formed in Tiraspol and Iași, later giving rise to the famous White Guard division.

They sang about that unit:

“From Romania on campaign came Drozdovsky’s glorious regiment,
to save the people it marched to fulfil its difficult duty.”
OLEG AIRAPETOV:
I think we have by now more or less identified the dividing line between a volunteer and a mercenary.

A volunteer is someone who goes to war for ideological reasons.

His motives are not material; his motives are spiritual.

He defends his own ideals.

If you like, he goes to war in order to destroy war.

A mercenary, by contrast, goes to war exclusively for material considerations; he lives by war.
If we recall one of the hymns of French mercenaries, it contains the words:

“Long live death, long live war, long live the valiant mercenary.”

I do not think any volunteer would agree to repeat the words of that French mercenary hymn.

That is the whole difference.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
When the war began in Transnistria, the exhausted Russian people, worn down by the disasters of the twentieth century — this super-ethnos — demonstrated that it was not yet completely dead, that it was still capable of certain vital impulses.

The cause of those impulses was a sense of dignity, a sense of ethnic solidarity.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
That is a profound and correct observation.
If we examine the history of the volunteer movement, at least outside Russia, we see that its social and ideological structure is extremely diverse.

People go there with completely different, and often opposing, views.

It was the same in Transnistria.

There were nationalists, communists and internationalists.

There were Russian nationalists and Ukrainian nationalists.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
I remember that reconnaissance in our company was commanded by a Ukrainian nationalist.

A trident was displayed on the stock of his assault rifle.

One of his subordinates was a Russian Orthodox ultramonarchist nicknamed “Kolya the Emperor.”

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
If we look at the volunteer movement of 1876, on the eve of the liberation war, we see that a very mixed assortment of volunteers gathered in Serbia.

There were monarchists, supporters of a Great Russia, liberals, and supporters of the revolutionary-democratic movement, often hostile to one another.
Why did they go there?

It seems to me that the initial impulse behind the volunteer movement, whose core is formed by passionaries, comes from protest against the reality a person sees at home but cannot change.

Secondly, there is an idealistic element.
He goes somewhere where this opposing ideal supposedly exists.

While the first motive can easily be translated into practice, the second is connected with romantic ideas and is doomed to collapse, because as a rule an ideal is incompatible with real life.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
In Transnistria one could observe how many people experienced the collapse of their ideals and transformed from volunteers into mercenaries.

In fairness, it must be said that by no means everyone who came to fight in Transnistria was a pure volunteer.

Alongside ideologically motivated fighters who tried, with weapons in their hands, to establish a higher truth and obtain justice for the Russian people, there were also quite a few outright lumpen elements.

Practically every platoon included characters nicknamed “Odessa.”

Transnistria is only a few dozen kilometres from Odessa, after all, and many such brave Odessans poured into this relatively prosperous territory simply in order to profit and loot.

I should say that the Transnistrian War was not the hardest war, so there was room there for criminals as well.

Many subsequently became professional mercenaries and went immediately afterwards to Karabakh, for example, or to Abkhazia.

But look at how tragically the fates of those who went to fight in Karabakh and Abkhazia developed.

Many people who had sat in the same trench in Transnistria later found themselves in opposing trenches and on opposing sides in those wars for various reasons.

Some went to fight for Azerbaijan, while others went to help the Christian Armenians.

IGOR STRELKOV:
I know people who went there not because of ideology.

Many of them said they were going there to gain experience that would later be useful to them here in Russia.

And those wars were much more serious than the Transnistrian War.

The losses were greater.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
What Igor has just said reminds me of an episode from Churchill’s biography, since Churchill was also a volunteer.

During the Greco-Turkish War he wrote to his mother asking her to obtain letters of recommendation for him.

There was a sentence along these lines:

“If you obtain letters of recommendation to the Greeks, I will go and fight for the Greeks; if you obtain them to the Turks, then I will fight for the Turks, because what I need is precisely this combat experience.”

For an officer, for a professional serviceman, it is natural to want to acquire this kind of experience.

But if we return once again to the distinction between mercenarism and volunteering, we can recall the 1970s and the end of the colonial conflicts in Africa.

At that time it seemed that the era of mercenaries was drawing to a close.

And every mercenary claimed to be going off to defend one idea or another.
The fact is that an ideological component is always present among mercenaries.

But it is not their principal motivation.

It serves as a cover.

VOLUNTEERS
(RADIO ZAVTRA)

PART 2

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
The Chechen War, which is regarded as a war in which professional Chechen fighters defeated an unfortunate Russian army made up of miserable conscripts, was in fact, to a considerable extent, a volunteer war on the federal side.
One of the participants in today’s programme, Igor, also went through the Chechen War as a contract soldier and volunteer.

IGOR STRELKOV (GIRKIN):
Most of the contract soldiers who fought in Chechnya — and many military units consisted of them, including the 166th, 205th and 131st Motor Rifle Brigades — were recruited through state structures, through military commissariats.

It should be remembered that most of my comrades came from Russia’s so-called Red Belt, where there was no work, factories stood idle, and in order to feed a family you either had to trade or engage in banditry.

For them, signing a contract and going to Chechnya may therefore have represented a way out of that situation.
There were also quite a lot of lumpen people who went to fight simply because they had nowhere else to go.

But I agree that there was also a fairly large number of volunteers — above all, of course, Cossacks from both the North Caucasus and other regions.

Despite the fact that the media denounced them as murderers, these people believed they were carrying out their duty.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Do you remember how the democratic press screamed about the beasts who were supposedly tearing poor, unfortunate Chechen children to pieces in Samashki?

Those “beasts,” as you know, lost more than thirty men killed in the battle for Samashki.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
It seems to me that when we speak about the Chechen War, particular attention should be paid to the regions that produced larger numbers of volunteers.

One was the Red Belt.

I believe the reasons there were predominantly social, although not exclusively so — it is not called the Red Belt by accident.
The second group consisted of the Cossack regions.

I believe the ideological war over Chechnya had been lost long before the military conflict began.

People even said that the “brilliant man,” Chechen propaganda minister Movladi Udugov, had defeated the federal propaganda system.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Of course he defeated it.
NTV was on his side...

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
It was not difficult to win when roughly ninety percent of airtime and practically all the leading press organs were working for him.

Against this stood the newspaper Zavtra and several other patriotic, comparatively small media outlets.

Nevertheless, the North Caucasus foreland produced a significant number of volunteers.

There was even a Cossack battalion.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Which became famous for exceptional bravery and, at times, almost insane attacks.

I remember an attack near Orekhovo in which the battalion lost twelve men in a single battle.

For the Chechen War, those were very substantial losses.

IGOR STRELKOV:
As far as fighting spirit is concerned, the battalion really was quite combat-capable.

It participated in fighting near Orekhovo, near Bamut and in Grozny during the closing days of the war.

It went into battle as an entire unit without requiring anyone to drive it forward.

Meanwhile, many motor-rifle units, consisting largely of conscripts, and even the 205th Brigade, in which half the men were contract soldiers, preferred to remain on duty at checkpoints and in garrisons and not stick their noses out.
The Cossacks, by contrast, went decisively into battle.

It is characteristic that the Yermolovsky Battalion never received heavy weapons.

Its most powerful weapons were 82-mm mortars.

Incidentally, I would like to draw attention to another phenomenon connected with volunteering — the events of 1993.

At that time, the army for the most part remained a passive observer of events, while small groups of volunteer fighters acted on both sides.

Here we can see a very concrete dividing line between volunteering and the army.
The army that remained passive then is now reaping the consequences of that passivity.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
In fact, what is happening is a completely natural process.

There was a large Soviet Army that had not fought wars for many years.

After the Soviet Union ceased to exist, Russia was simply unable materially to maintain armed forces of that size.

It seemed that we no longer needed the old army, while a new army existed only as a vague project.
To paraphrase Saltykov-Shchedrin: the new has not yet been born, the old has not yet died, and meanwhile both are still breathing.

One indication of the critical sickness of our armed forces is the enormous number of special units.

When the Russian Imperial Army was dying and disintegrating in 1917–1918, an enormous number of special units also appeared.

When there are many special forces units, it means the other units are becoming incapable of fighting.

Only a handful of those who wear military insignia are actually prepared to fight — in other words, volunteers.

AND THE ETERNAL BATTLE

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
The issue of volunteering is especially relevant and acute today precisely because the state is on the verge of collapse.

Society needs protection, but there is no one to protect it.

There are individual special forces units whose commanders are looking in different directions.

And there is a certain mass of people who have been through regional wars and acquired combat experience.

These people are potential volunteers — and unfortunately quite a few are potential mercenaries as well.

But there is another purely volunteer war in modern Russian history.

That is the war in Serbia.
Not a particularly large number of people went there, but nevertheless those people upheld the honour of our Motherland and gave Russians — all of us — a chance to justify ourselves.

We can at least say that in some way we helped the brotherly Serbian Slavic people.

IGOR STRELKOV:
In reality there were at most several hundred volunteers in Serbia.

Russian volunteer units normally numbered no more than ten to twenty-five men.

These units operated on different fronts and did not coordinate their actions with one another.

There were many individuals who reached Serbia independently and did not find Russian units.

Those men served in purely Serbian units, both in Bosnia and in Serbian Krajina, and fought on various fronts.

Nothing is known about many of them.

One encounters relatives of people killed there who are looking for their loved ones’ former comrades but cannot find them, because those men went to Serbia and fought somewhere outside the Russian detachments.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
How did the Serbs treat the Russians, and how did the Russians fight?

IGOR STRELKOV:
They fought very well — compared with the Serbs.
The Russians really did fight better and inflicted greater losses on the enemy in battle.

However, as far as I know, no Russian — at least none of those with whom I had contact — and certainly no Russian detachment took part in ethnic cleansing.

Such cleansing was, of course, organised by the Serbs, just as it was by the Croats and Muslims.

That really belongs to the Balkan style of warfare, where a person of another religion is regarded as not quite human.

It is a medieval tradition.

But the Muslim and Croatian atrocities were probably worse.

The Russians were regarded as a shock force, perhaps even as a psychological one.

When two or three Russian soldiers went forward with the Serbs, the Serbs would immediately begin loudly announcing it over the radio and simply shouting it.

That had a certain psychological effect on the enemy.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Let us remember that the great Russian Empire once came to the aid of the Serbian people and solved the Balkan problem for a time through the strength of the mighty Russian Army.

That army swept into the Balkans and, after the first battles, which were not always successful, eventually defeated the Turks and reached the gates of Tsargrad — Constantinople.
Unfortunately, because of purely international complications, Constantinople was never occupied by Russian troops.

Nevertheless, Russian forces stood on its very doorstep.

Today, unfortunately, our modern state — the Russian Federation — is incapable of pursuing a nationally oriented policy because it currently has a completely different ruling elite.

That is why the war in Serbia has been lost.

That is why the Americans are free to bomb whomever they want in the Balkans.

That is why volunteers remain the only hope not merely of the Serbian people, but now of the Russian people as well.

Anti-national forces inside the country are carefully trying to drive the Russian volunteer movement — which genuinely exists and possesses serious personnel — into the criminal underground.

People who know how to handle weapons, who possess enormous experience and who are prepared to fight for the Motherland are to be brought under criminal law.

They are to be declared mercenaries.
Society is to be told that they are immoral people, that they are beasts, and clear instructions are to be given on how to punish and imprison them if these people should suddenly stand up in defence of Russian national interests somewhere inside the country or beyond its borders — for example, let us say, in Northern Kazakhstan.

IGOR STRELKOV:
The issue is not even that the state wants to punish or intimidate these people.

These people are quite difficult to intimidate.
They have already seen death.

For many of them prison is of course worse than death, but they have already crossed a certain threshold.

What they are trying to do is intimidate others.

They are trying to intimidate thousands of potential participants in a national liberation movement.

Thousands of people tried to go to Serbia.

They wrote letters, wore out the doorsteps of the Serbian embassy and consulates, and tried through Cossack and patriotic organisations to find channels through which they could travel to Serbia and take up arms.

I know that very many people also came to the newspaper Zavtra.

This law is aimed precisely at them.

Its purpose is to ensure that the volunteer movement, which has not yet developed on a large scale, remains no more than small groups of veterans of regional conflicts.

Others are supposed to regard them as mercenaries and under no circumstances join the core that genuinely exists.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
It seems to me that there is another aspect here — an ideological one.

The democratic media need to construct an image of negative behaviour.
They need to show what a person should not be like.

A sincere desire and ability to defend the interests of one’s Fatherland and one’s people — this is precisely what represents a danger to a significant part of the mass media, meaning both state and private structures engaged in ideological warfare.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
I want to say that these media and a significant portion of the so-called democratic establishment are now fighting not merely against the word “patriot,” but against every manifestation of genuine social activity.

OLEG AIRAPETOV:
In other words, they are fighting not against the form, but against the substance.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
Yes, now they are.

Because liberal ideology has suffered an obvious collapse and is no longer valued throughout the post-Soviet space and Russia, the word “patriot” had to be legalised and introduced into common usage.

It became acceptable and perfectly respectable.

There is now only one question:

Will patriotism become the same kind of semantic abstraction as the ideals of liberalism and democracy?

The prospects of the volunteer movement in Russia are tied to the prospects for Russia’s very existence — to whether a Russian state will continue to exist at all.

Today we have a completely ruined army, relatively combat-capable Interior Troops and a looming large-scale conflict — for example, in the North Caucasus.

War there is simply inevitable.

We will meet that war with our bare hands.

There will be no one to defend the population of southern Russia except the population itself.
Many Russian people living in those regions — in Stavropol Territory and Krasnodar Territory — understand this very well.

They are already stockpiling weapons, taking up arms and conducting active, intensive training.

IGOR STRELKOV:
Calling it “active, intensive combat training” is perhaps a bit strong.

But such tendencies really do exist.

And Article 359 of the Criminal Code on mercenarism, as well as Article 222 on illegal possession and carrying of weapons, strikes above all at Russian people.

Today in Dagestan, Ossetia, Ingushetia and other national republics, legalised self-defence units and national organisations such as the “Wild Division” possess not merely assault rifles and machine guns, but armoured personnel carriers, mortars and anti-aircraft weapons.

Yet for some reason throughout the North Caucasus, the people prosecuted for “possession and carrying of weapons” are Russians, and above all Cossacks.

This happens especially often where the law-enforcement agencies consist mainly of people originating from the Caucasus itself.

Russian people who nevertheless join self-defence detachments and prepare for war are, in principle, already volunteers.

They will simply have to fight not somewhere abroad, but at home.

They have only one choice:

leave and abandon their lands, or fight for them.

They choose to fight, as every self-respecting citizen of Russia and every self-respecting man should — to fight for his home and his family.

Here, in southern Russia, volunteering may therefore take on an entirely new character.

ALEXANDER BORODAI:
To sum up, I can say that we all turned out to be entirely in agreement that there is simply no one except volunteers who can save Russia.

Therefore, let us hope that the volunteer movement in Russia, despite all the efforts of the mass media, will not die but will continue to exist and develop.

And in conclusion I would like to recall lines from the volunteer march of the Kornilov Regiment:

“The bells of ancient Moscow will ring,
and Russian troops will enter it in ranks.”

I believe that those troops will indeed enter Moscow.

And I believe that those troops will consist mainly of volunteers.

THE VIBE MANUFACTURING PLAYBOOK

1. Measure everything. Digital calipers for small parts, a phone LiDAR app like Polycam to scan a space or an object. Bad measurements are the #1 reason first builds fail

2. Have a frontier model write the design as code. Describe the part to a model like Claude Opus 5.5 or Astra, and have it write the design in a codebased CAD tool like OpenSCAD or CadQuery. Zoo's Text to CAD does it in one step!

3. Use real CAD files. The text to 3D models on Hugging Face make shapes that look right, but factories need precise files: STEP for machined parts, DXF for lasercut metal, STL for 3D printing

4. Make sure it can be made. Ask the AI to check the design against how factories actually work: how tight metal can bend, how small a hole can be, how much wiggle room parts need etc...

5. Prototype in plastic first. A $300 to $600 home 3D printer like a Bambu Lab lets you test the fit overnight before paying for metal (really fun to play with too!)

6. Pay an engineer for 1 hour. Before your first real order, have a mechanical engineer on Upwork etc review the files. It's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

7. Send it out. SendCutSend cuts and bends metal, Xometry and Protolabs handle machining and plastic, JLCPCB builds circuit boards. Instant quotes, and parts usually ship in days.

8. Add the brains. Most smart features run on a cheap wifi chip like the ESP32. Design the board in KiCad, and use ESPHome to control it straight from your phone.

9. Make one, then fix it. Your first version will be off somewhere! Order a single unit, test it, and adjust.

10. Do the math. Add up parts, finishing, assembly, packaging, and shipping. Custom products are hard to resell, so price for healthy margins.

11. Sell the design and make to order. Let customers adjust the measurements, and only manufacture after they pay. Zero warehouse, zero unsold stock.

12. Handle the boring part. If it plugs into a wall or touches kids, you'll need safety certification. It's slow and annoying, which is exactly why it's a moat.

13. Scale when it works. Once orders are steady, switch to batch runs and your cost per unit drops fast.

Vibe coding changed who can build software!

Vibe manufacturing is about to change who can build things!!

Even if you just want to make things for yourself (and not make things for others)
