text:
CompTIA SY0-701 Security+ 

Domains:
1. General Security Concepts
2. Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations
3. Security Architecture 
4. Security Operations 
5. Security Program Management and Oversight 

Notes in 🧵
@grok with the assist 🙌
Practice PBQs coming soon!

Domain 3.0 — Security Architecture (18%)

3.1 Models

Infrastructure as a service: you secure the operating system, applications, and data. Platform as a service: applications and data. Software as a service: data and access. The provider always secures the physical plant. A responsibility matrix is the document that records that split. It is not an architecture.
Serverless means the provider runs execution, scaling, and networking. You still secure the code and the data. Infrastructure as code means you define the infrastructure in code. Hybrid is cloud plus on-premises. Virtualization runs multiple operating systems on one host. A container shares the host kernel. Microservices increase east-west traffic and make access control more granular. Software-defined networking separates network control from the hardware.
Centralized is one control point. Decentralized spreads control. Cloud is services over the internet. On-premises can be either.
For embedded systems, industrial control systems, SCADA, and a real-time operating system, availability and safety beat aggressive patching. The concern is the inability to patch. Use compensating controls and isolation. A real-time operating system may drop buffer-overflow protections for speed. A snowflake system is a unique handmade build that drifts from the baseline. An air gap is physical isolation, the strongest and the hardest to patch. A VLAN is logical segmentation, not an air gap.
The cloud-compute concern is isolation between instances. Easy deployment still has to integrate with existing security controls. Encrypt traffic in transit to external applications.

3.2 Infrastructure

Fail-closed blocks traffic when the device fails. That favors security. Fail-open allows it. That favors availability. An inline device can block. A tap or SPAN port only copies, so it can detect but not stop the packet.
A packet filter looks at stateless headers. A stateful firewall tracks connections. A proxy terminates the session and starts a new one. A next-generation firewall adds application awareness, deep inspection, and identity. A unified threat management box bundles firewall, intrusion prevention, antivirus, and VPN, and it can add latency. A web application firewall is Layer 7 HTTP and HTTPS only. A known web flaw you cannot patch yet needs that firewall, not a network intrusion prevention system. An intrusion detection system alerts and adds little latency.
Security zones separate employee and guest access. TLS encrypts the channel, not the data after it arrives. Port security restricts by MAC address. 802.1X authenticates the port, usually with RADIUS. Filtering by IP and port is Layer 4. Layer 3 is routing. Layer 2 is MAC.
IPSec is the tunneling suite. Authentication Header is integrity only. Encapsulating Security Payload encrypts. Software-defined WAN is centralized WAN control, on-premises or cloud. Secure access service edge is cloud-delivered networking plus security. Extensible Authentication Protocol is an authentication framework, not a tunnel.
A jump server is the admin gateway. A proxy hides the client and reduces the public-facing surface. A load balancer spreads the same work. Reducing the paths in is attack-surface reduction, not an inline device. A TLS VPN secures the tunnel, not the remote endpoint. A screened subnet, or DMZ, keeps a compromised public server off the internal network.

Open Systems Interconnection layers, from the wire up. Security+ mostly uses 2, 3, 4, and 7.

7 — Application. The interface a program uses for the network. HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SMTP, FTP, and SSH live here. A web application firewall works at this layer.
6 — Presentation. Formats the data for the application: encryption, compression, and encoding. TLS is often placed here or at Layer 5, though the exam usually treats HTTPS as Layer 7.
5 — Session. Opens, manages, and closes the conversation between two applications. It handles the dialogue, not the routing.
4 — Transport. End-to-end delivery between processes. TCP is reliable and connection-oriented. UDP is fast and connectionless. Ports live here. Filtering by IP and port is a Layer 4 decision.
3 — Network. Logical addressing and routing between networks. IP, ICMP, and routers live here. A packet filter that only looks at IP addresses is Layer 3.
2 — Data link. Local delivery on one segment. MAC addresses, switches, VLANs, and port security live here. Frames, not packets.
1 — Physical. The bits on the medium: cable, fiber, radio, connectors, and signaling. An air gap is a physical control. A VLAN is not.

3.3 Data

At rest means stored. In transit means moving. In use means being processed, so it is in memory and harder to encrypt. Sovereignty is the law of the place where the data sits. A geographic restriction keeps data in an allowed region. That is not diversification.
Regulated data is required by law, such as health, card, or financial data. Confidential fits nondisclosure-agreement data. Critical hurts operations if lost. Public is unrestricted. Also expect sensitive, private, and restricted. Intellectual property covers trade secrets, patents, and copyrights. Copyright protects original works. Non-human-readable data needs a machine. Human-readable data can be read directly.
Encryption provides confidentiality. A digital signature provides integrity and non-repudiation. Together they give both. Masking hides personal data and keeps the format for analysis or test data. Tokenization replaces the value with a substitute held in a vault. Hashing is one-way and proves integrity. It does not conceal stored data and it is not reversible, so it is not a substitute for encryption. General Data Protection Regulation-compliant handling is the multinational personal-data answer. Secure boot with signed images stops unauthorized firmware. That protects the system, not the data classification.

3.4 Resilience

Recovery point objective is the maximum acceptable data loss, so it drives backup frequency. Recovery time objective is the maximum acceptable downtime and must be at or under the maximum tolerable downtime. Mean time to repair is average repair time. Mean time between failures is reliability.
A hot site is ready now. A warm site has equipment, and the data lags. A cold site is space and power only. Onsite stays in the same building and shares the disaster. Offsite is another location. Encrypt backups before transport. A copy without encryption still exposes the data, including to ransomware that steals the backup.
A full backup is everything. An incremental backup is changes since the last backup of any type. A differential backup is changes since the last full backup. A snapshot is a fast point-in-time image, often on the same storage, and it is not a backup by itself. Continuous backups fit many reverts per day. Replication is a real-time copy, so it also copies corruption. Journaling can recover to the exact failure point.
Load balancing sends the same work to many servers. Clustering groups nodes so another node takes over. One failure should not drop the service. A design that assigns different tasks, so one failure drops that feature, is neither. Parallel processing tests recovery beside production without cutting over. A tabletop exercise is discussion only. A simulation is a practiced outage, not red versus blue. Failover is the actual switch. Geographic dispersion avoids one regional disaster. Platform diversity and multi-cloud avoid one vendor or stack.
A UPS is short battery power. A generator is long fuel power. A complete loss needs both. Voltage regulators and power distribution units do not keep systems up. Capacity planning forecasts people, technology, and infrastructure. Untested recovery is not a control.

Domain 4.0 — Security Operations (28%)

4.1 Hardening and baselines

Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain
A baseline is the documented minimum secure configuration every system of a given type must meet before production and keep meeting afterward. Sources are CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, and vendor guides (Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit), customized for the environment.
Establish means write and      approve the standard. That includes encryption, firewall rules, access      control, disabled services, password policy, and logging. Logging is part      of the baseline, not a later step.
Deploy means push it. Use a      golden image, Group Policy, or configuration management, then verify it      landed.
Maintain means patch, watch for      configuration drift, and update the baseline when vulnerabilities,      software, or policy change. This is where real breaches happen.
Operational practice that matches exam scenarios: harden the OS and apply the baseline before you put the host on the network or hand it over. That is deployment hygiene, not the definition of “establish.”
Mobile and wireless
Mobile priority controls are full-device encryption, screen lock, MDM policy, and the ability to remote lock or remote wipe a lost device. On BYOD, also segment corporate data (container/MAM) so a wipe can target work data. Related models: COPE, CYOD, COBO.
Wireless points that are correct:
WEP is broken. TKIP is weak and      deprecated. Do not choose either.
WPA2 uses the 4-way handshake.      An attacker can capture it and offline-brute a weak PSK. Cipher is      AES-CCMP.
WPA3-Personal uses SAE      (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, Dragonfly), a Diffie-Hellman-style      exchange. No hash of the PSK goes over the air, so offline dictionary      attacks fail. It also gives forward secrecy and a unique session key per      client even when the passphrase is shared.
WPA3 requires protected      management frames (802.11w). Open networks use Enhanced Open / OWE so      traffic is encrypted without a password.
Site survey and heat map before      you place APs. Disable WPS. Put guests on a separate SSID with client      isolation.
Hardening targets and apps
Server hardening is least privilege, patching, removing unused roles and accounts, and a locked-down baseline. There is no single “first”; both privilege and patching are expected answers.
Router and switch hardening: SSH instead of Telnet, SNMPv3 instead of v1/v2c, strong credentials, unused ports and services off, and ACLs on the management plane. Changing IPs for obscurity is not a control.
ICS/SCADA and HMI: the exam concern is unauthorized access (often default credentials), plus network segmentation. Availability usually outranks aggressive patching.
Unknown or untrusted software goes in a sandbox. For SQL injection and XSS, the primary fix is server-side input validation (and output encoding for XSS). A WAF is a compensating control; it does not replace validation.
Quick traps: “establish” is not “apply updates later,” WPA3 is SAE not the 4-way handshake, and obscurity is never the router answer.

4.2 Assets

Assignment and tracking
Inventory is the current list of hardware, software, and data: what you have, where it is, and who owns it. It is continuous, not a one-time count. Missing items are shadow IT.
Enumeration is the detailed discovery behind that list. It identifies systems and components (a laptop is also CPU, memory, disks, and peripherals) and keeps the record current as assets change. It is more than a headcount. It is not specifically the access-control list. Access is handled by ownership, classification, and least privilege.
Classification labels sensitivity and the handling level that follows (public, internal, confidential, restricted). Ownership names the accountable person. That is what routes patches, incidents, and residual risk, and it reduces unowned insider exposure. The owner accepts risk; the custodian (often IT) maintains the asset.
Disposal
You have sanitization and destruction the right way around now.
Sanitization removes data so it      cannot be recovered. The device can still be reused. Methods: overwrite      (HDDs; clearing for internal reuse, purge for leaving custody),      crypto-erase (destroy the key on an SSD or self-encrypting drive that was      encrypted the whole time), and degaussing (magnetic media only: HDD, tape.      Useless on SSD, flash, and optical).
Destruction is physical:      industrial shred, pulverize, incinerate, or disintegrate. The media is no      longer usable. Use this for the highest sensitivity. A hammer or drill can      destroy a few platters in a lab, but the exam answer is industrial      destruction, not a casual smash that can leave readable fragments.
Certification is the record. A      staff member watching is not proof. You still want a certificate of      destruction or a sanitization log (method, date, serial, responsible      party).
Retention is how long you must      keep data for legal or business reasons, then dispose. “Keep it forever”      is not a retention schedule.
SSD trap: degauss does nothing, and a single overwrite can miss blocks because of wear leveling. Prefer crypto-erase if it was always encrypted, otherwise physical destruction.

4.3 Vulnerability management

Identification and scoring
CVE names the flaw. The ID is CVE-2022-12345, not the year-number alone. CVSS scores it. A string like CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H is the vector, not the identifier.
Base-score bands:
0.1–3.9 Low
4.0–6.9 Medium
7.0–8.9 High
9.0–10.0 Critical
Do not map “hard to exploit plus severe impact” to High, or “easier / sensitive systems” to Critical. Attack complexity and impact are inputs to the formula. High complexity lowers the score, so severe impact that is hard to exploit often lands in Medium or High, not automatically High. Critical is only a score of 9.0–10.0. Sensitivity of your systems is an environmental adjustment, not the definition of Critical.
False positive: alert, no real issue. False negative: real issue, no alert. False negatives are worse.
OSINT is legally available public information. The dark web is hidden (Tor and similar), not automatically illegal. Exam use is threat intel: stolen credentials, exploit sales, chatter. A vulnerability scan identifies. A pen test tries to exploit. Package monitoring watches dependencies and libraries for known vulnerable versions. Responsible disclosure and bug bounties are the other identification paths.
Response
An exception or exemption delays or skips the fix and must record the accepted risk and the owner. A compensating control is the substitute when the primary control cannot be applied (segmentation, WAF, extra monitoring). Insurance transfers financial impact. It does not remediate the flaw.
Exposure factor is the percent of asset value lost in one incident. Single loss expectancy is asset value times exposure factor.
Confirm the fix by rescanning. Audit and independent verification are the other validation methods. A third-party test can be that verification, but the objective terms are rescan, audit, and verification.

4.4 Monitoring

Activities and tools
Log aggregation collects logs and normalizes formats so they can be compared. It does not correlate or decide an attack. Monitoring is the continuous watching. Alerting is the notice that a rule matched. Alert tuning cuts noise. Reporting is the output.
SIEM aggregates, correlates across sources, and alerts. SOAR runs playbooks: enrich, isolate, ticket, notify. “Automate the response” is SOAR, not SIEM.
SCAP is the automation framework (OVAL, XCCDF, CVE, and related languages) used to check configurations and vulnerabilities. A benchmark is the standard you compare against, such as a CIS Benchmark or a DISA STIG. SCAP can express a benchmark. It is not the benchmark.
NetFlow (and IPFIX) summarizes flows: source, destination, ports, bytes, duration. It does not carry payload, and it does not name the attack. An analyst or a detection rule does that. SNMP polls device status and sends traps. It is a management protocol, not encryption. Prefer SNMPv3. Versions 1 and 2c send community strings in the clear.
Data the logs actually contain
A packet capture is the full packet as sent. If the session is TLS, you see headers and ciphertext, not the decrypted application data, unless you have the keys. If it is cleartext, the payload is there. Do not treat “pcap shows headers only” as the rule. Full content is the pcap. Summary is NetFlow.
File metadata is data about the file: creator or owner, size, created, and modified, sometimes last access. It is not the content, and it is not a list of who opened the file. That comes from access or audit logs.
Firewall logs show the connection that was seen: source, destination, ports, action, and time. They do not inventory open ports on the destination. That is a scan.
Quarantine isolates a file or host so it can be analyzed. It does not delete it. Archiving is long-term retention. It is not faster search. Hot SIEM storage is what you search. Archive is what you keep for the retention period.

4.5 Enterprise controls

Detection and web controls
An IDS detects and alerts. It is usually passive, on a span or tap. An IPS sits inline and can block. Fail-open keeps traffic flowing if the IPS dies. Fail-closed stops it.
An NGFW is application-aware and can tie rules to user identity, not just ports. A UTM is the all-in-one box: firewall, IPS, antivirus, and content filtering. A WAF is specifically for web-application attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting.
A secure web gateway filters URLs, can apply time-of-day rules, and inspects user web traffic for malware. A centralized proxy gives every branch the same policy and the same reports. An agent-based filter travels with the remote device, so the laptop is still filtered when it is not on the corporate network.
NAC
You have the agents the right way around. Agent-based NAC installs software and reports richer posture: patches, antivirus, disk encryption, and running processes. Agentless NAC uses network methods such as 802.1X, DHCP fingerprinting, or scanning, and needs no install. It sees less.
NAC checks posture before or as the device connects, then allows, denies, or quarantines. 802.1X authenticates the device or user on the port before the port opens. NAC often uses 802.1X, but posture is the extra check.
Email, DLP, and placement
SPF lists the servers allowed to send for a domain. DKIM signs the message so it can be checked for tampering. DMARC is the policy for SPF or DKIM failure: none, quarantine, or reject, plus reports. S/MIME uses certificates to sign and encrypt the message itself. TLS encrypts the path between mail servers. It does not protect the message after delivery.
DLP inspects outbound email and files for sensitive data. Blocking every attachment is too broad. An any-to-any outbound allow is not a secure firewall rule.
A screened subnet, also called a DMZ, holds public servers between the outside and the internal network. A GPO linked to an organizational unit applies that department’s rights. SELinux is mandatory access control that restricts Linux processes. A web reputation score is a site’s trustworthiness, used to allow or block before a full content scan.

4.6 IAM

Account lifecycle
User provisioning creates the account and assigns rights. Deprovisioning on offboarding is an immediate disable or removal, not a waiting period. Resource provisioning is capacity: virtual machines, storage, and cloud resources. Do not swap those answers.
Attestation is the owner periodically confirming that access is still appropriate. Identity proofing confirms the person is real before the credential is issued.
Just-in-time permissions and ephemeral credentials exist only for the task, then expire. Temporal accounts are the time-limited account version of the same idea. A passkey is passwordless public-key authentication, usually FIDO2. A biometric or a PIN unlocks the private key on the device. The server never sees a password or the private key.
Passwords and factors
Map the control to the failure:
A password manager addresses too      many passwords.
A unique-password rule addresses      reuse.
Complexity and length address      guessing and dictionary attacks.
Expiration addresses stale      passwords. The exam still tests this, even though current guidance prefers      length and breach checks.
Multifactor authentication      limits damage from a stolen or reused password. It does not stop reuse.
A software token is an app code. A hard token is a physical code device. A security key is the device you insert or tap. Somewhere you are is location, such as GPS or a network location. Something you are is the biometric.
Federation
Single sign-on is one authentication for many applications, and it is the usual interoperability answer inside an organization. Federation is the trust that extends that across organizations. LDAP is the directory protocol, not the login. SAML is the enterprise federation assertion. OAuth is authorization, meaning delegated access. OpenID Connect is authentication built on top of OAuth. If the question says “let this app access the account without the password,” choose OAuth. If it says “prove who the user is across companies,” choose SAML or OpenID Connect.

4.7 Automation

Guard rails are automated policy limits on a workflow. They block a bad change before it lands, such as a public storage bucket or a mass delete. They are not physical barriers.
Enforcing baselines and standard configurations is how automation stops configuration drift. The same build runs every time. Continuous integration and testing catch defects early and speed delivery. Scripting user provisioning is the onboarding case: create the account, assign groups, and disable it on exit. Resource provisioning is the infrastructure version.
A workforce multiplier is the small team plus automation covering work that would otherwise need more people. Employee retention means the repetitive work is gone, so people stay. It is not the control that preserves automation knowledge. That risk sits under ongoing supportability: the scripts need skilled people who can maintain them, regardless of how popular the vendor is.
One automation platform is a single point of failure. If it stops, provisioning and response stop, and availability suffers. If it is compromised, the attacker inherits its privileges. The other considerations are complexity, cost, and technical debt from scripts that hide a problem instead of fixing it.

4.8 Incident response

The SY0-701 sequence is preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Analysis sits between detection and containment. Detection finds and triages the event. Analysis determines scope, impact, and what you are dealing with. Then contain, then eradicate, then recover. Lessons learned is last, after the incident is closed.
Root-cause analysis explains why it happened and what stops a repeat. That is analysis or lessons learned, not detection. Threat hunting is proactive: assume the attacker may already be inside and go look, rather than waiting for an alert.
Forensics terms:
Acquisition is the unaltered      copy, taken in order of volatility. Memory and running state before disk,      disk before remote logs and backups.
Preservation keeps that copy      unchanged. Hashes are how you prove it.
Chain of custody records every      handler, from collection through court.
Legal hold stops deletion so      evidence survives.
E-discovery is producing that      electronic data for a legal case.
The report follows the audience.      Executives get impact and decisions. Technical staff get indicators and      scope. Legal gets custody and handling.

4.9 Investigation sources

Firewall logs show source and destination IP, ports, action, and time. They do not list every open port on the target. OS security logs show successful and failed authentications, account changes, and process or privilege events. Application logs show what that app saw: failed logins with user, time, and IP. They do not contain GPS. Endpoint logs add the process, file, and user on that host. IPS and IDS logs show the signature and the traffic that matched. Network logs and NetFlow show who talked to whom. A packet capture is the full packet when you need payload. Metadata is data about the file or message, not its contents.
Correlate on time, IP, user, and process across those sources. One log rarely answers the question. Vulnerability scans, dashboards, and automated reports support the investigation. They are not a substitute for the event logs.

text:
The debate surrounding #Starlink in #India is not really about internet speeds, rural connectivity or even Elon Musk.

It is about #sovereignty 
History teaches us that nations rarely lose strategic autonomy overnight. More often, dependence develops gradually through systems, networks and institutions that become too important to function without.

The #BritishEastIndiaCompany did not arrive in India as a conquering army. It arrived as a commercial enterprise promising trade, access to global markets and economic opportunity. Over time, commercial influence evolved into political leverage, strategic control and eventually colonial rule.

The world of the 21st century is different, but the underlying principle remains relevant.

Today, influence is exercised not only through territory and military power but through data, communications infrastructure, digital platforms, satellite networks and technological dependence.

This is where Starlink becomes a strategic question rather than merely a telecommunications project.

Supporters correctly point out that satellite internet can transform connectivity in remote regions, improve disaster response and bridge digital divides. These are real benefits.

However, strategic planners must also ask a different set of questions:
“Who controls the network?
Who ultimately decides where service is available?”

What happens during a geopolitical crisis?
Can a sovereign nation guarantee uninterrupted access if the infrastructure is owned, operated and controlled by a foreign private entity?

The Ukraine conflict offers a powerful example.
Reports revealed that Starlink services were restricted during a planned Ukrainian operation targeting Russian naval assets near Crimea. The result was that the operation could not proceed as intended because the communications network required for execution was unavailable.

Regardless of one’s views on the decision, the larger geopolitical lesson is clear:
A private company and its leadership possessed the ability to influence the operational options available to a sovereign state during an active conflict.

That reality should concern every serious strategic planner in the world.
The issue is not whether Elon Musk was right or wrong.

The issue is whether any nation should place critical national communications infrastructure in a position where ultimate operational control rests outside its sovereign authority.

For India, this question carries even greater significance.

India faces an increasingly contested security environment stretching from the Himalayas to the Indian Ocean. #Communications resilience is not merely an economic requirement; it is a #nationalsecurity necessity.

This does not mean rejecting foreign technology.
India has benefited enormously from international investment, technology partnerships and global integration.

But integration should never become dependence.
The ideal outcome is not isolation but strategic balance: encouraging innovation while ensuring robust regulatory oversight, #dataprotection, local compliance requirements and #sovereigncontrol mechanisms.

The lesson of the #EastIndiaCompany is often misunderstood.
The danger was never trade itself.

The danger was allowing critical leverage to accumulate outside Indian control.

As technology becomes the new arena of geopolitical competition, nations must remember a simple principle:
Infrastructure creates dependence.
Dependence creates leverage.
Leverage creates influence.

And influence, if left unchecked, can eventually challenge sovereignty itself.

India was colonised once through commerce and influence.
The next challenge, if it ever comes, will not arrive on sailing ships.

It will arrive through networks, platforms, satellites and systems that become too important to question

That is why the Starlink debate is not merely abt connectivity.
It is about ensuring that 🇮🇳’s digital future remains firmly under Indian sovereign control #JaiHind

Elon Musk's Starlink has secured agreements with India's leading telecom operators, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel, to introduce satellite-based internet services across the country. These partnerships aim to enhance connectivity, especially in remote and underserved regions where traditional internet infrastructure is lacking. 

The collaboration with Reliance Jio will leverage Jio's extensive retail network to distribute and install Starlink devices, utilizing existing telecom infrastructure to improve satellite coverage nationwide. Similarly, the agreement with Bharti Airtel focuses on integrating Starlink services with Airtel's network and retail channels, aiming to bridge the digital divide in India's remote and mountainous areas. 

Both partnerships are pending regulatory approval, as Starlink awaits its operating license in India—a process that has experienced delays due to national security considerations. These strategic moves underscore a significant effort to overcome India's digital divide, particularly in regions where traditional internet infrastructure is limited. 

However, challenges remain, notably regarding pricing. Starlink's services are priced at a premium compared to India's highly competitive mobile data market, which could affect adoption rates. Additionally, the dense population in rural India may pose challenges to the cost-benefit ratio of satellite-based internet services compared to rapidly expanding low-cost 5G services. 

These developments come after discussions between Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Elon Musk, highlighting the government's interest in leveraging advanced technologies to boost connectivity and technological innovation in the country.

Tesla and Starlink have sought entry into India for years. Tesla was blocked by a 110% tariff and local manufacturing rules, while Starlink faced national security concerns.  

With Trump back, things have turned into a cakewalk for Elon. The EV import tariff dropped from 110% to 15%, opening doors for Tesla, and Starlink is also making inroads. This seems to be a result of diplomatic arm-twisting rather than mutual benefit.  

Still, I see a blessing in disguise wrt Tesla, especially for consumers. High tariffs are primarily imposed to help domestic manufacturers grow and make the country self-reliant. We gave a lot of space for Tatas, Marutis, Mahindras, etc., to grow, innovate, and dominate, even at the cost of Indian consumers paying to protect substandard products and keep out competitive alternatives.  

If local manufacturers still can't compete, so be it. The entry-level Tesla will cost less than 40 lakh and has much better specs, performance, range, and battery life than any domestic EV. Why should Indian consumers be denied that when even Chinese companies are selling cars in India?  

Starlink, however, is a potentially risky deal if not diligently regulated, primarily due to the threat to our digital sovereignty. If its per-consumer cost is lower than Jio's and Airtel's current rates, local ISPs will be wiped out, creating a duopoly. If Jio and Airtel shift much of their traffic to Starlink, we’d be at its mercy, Musk could cut off our internet, suppress counterviews, and ban users at will. He could also refuse to block content harmful to national security.

This is not a compliance dispute. Expected deeper research from @ARKInvest  on this one. @wintonARK 's Starlink thesis has holes that spectrum law and physics won't let you ignore. If a fund this caliber is missing the fundamentals of D2D, it shows how poorly understood this space still is.
Let me address it directly.
His core claim: $SPCX  becomes the first truly global telecom, launches its own cellular brand, satellite-default with cellular failover.

Four problems.
1) Spectrum is sovereign. To run a global cellular brand, SpaceX needs direct-to-consumer spectrum in every country. Each nation licenses its own. You can't "amortize connectivity across the world" when you need 195 separate national grants and most governments won't hand a foreign company their citizens' airwaves. India just blocked Starlink for this exact reason. Europe reserved spectrum for local operators. Japan is building its own.
2) The capacity math is backwards. "Satellite default, cellular failover" violates physics. One satellite beam covers hundreds of square miles, sharing capacity across everyone in it. A cell tower covers a few hundred meters with orders of magnitude more capacity. Satellite can't be the DEFAULT in any populated area - there isn't enough capacity density. @SpaceX 's own VP said it: Starlink Mobile is "not meant to replace terrestrial infrastructure."
3) Sovereignty is moving the opposite direction. Your thesis needs governments to allow one foreign company to own national connectivity. That's exactly what's being blocked worldwide right now. The trend isn't toward a global SpaceX telecom - it's away from it.
4) Carriers won't be the failover. "Failover to cellular" needs roaming deals with the carriers SpaceX is trying to replace. Why would @ATT &T let SpaceX use its network as a backup for a product built to disintermediate AT&T? They wouldn't. That's why all 3 US carriers formed a JV around $ASTS instead - a partner that extends them, not one that replaces them.

The global telecom future is real. But it's not one company owning the world's connectivity. It's local carriers, sovereign spectrum, and a satellite layer that works THROUGH them. That's the model $ASTS  was built for. And it's the model governments are actively choosing.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.

Breaking :

EU Council wants to abolish correspondence secrecy

The EU member states want to abolish the modern secrecy of letters. In  the EU Council, the police should be able to prosecute private chat  flows and monitor such a letter communication. Experts warn that Signal  and WhatsApp could leave the EU.

The EU of citizens' rights – has this combination of words already  been heard? But the EU of governments, which is well there. The  elections in Belgium were held in parallel with the EU elections on 9.  held in June and ended with a triumph for the Flemish right-wing  conservatives (N-VA) and the Vlaams Belang. Liberal Prime Minister  Alexander De Croo immediately declared his resignation, but remains in  office. Its centre-left coalition will probably not be once again after  the losses suffered.

But now the country could end up one last coup in EU Brussels. Until  the 1. The Belgian Government holds the semi-annual Presidency of the EU  Council in July. Since the beginning of the year, the De Croo  government has been trying to enforce general chat control in the EU,  especially at end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp or Signal.  EU bodies have been planning this advance for a long time. So far, there  have been one or two vetoos too much in the Council. But now France had  itself break out of the blocking minority. And so the Belgian proposal  could already be adopted in the Council on Wednesday.

The Regulation includes the title of "Rules to combat child abuse".  It is supposedly about images that record child abuse (child sexual  abuse material, CSAM), and also sent internet links should be scanned  automatically. Ultimately, it is about access to the online  communication of citizens. The laudable fight against child pornography  is the giant hammer, with which the small nail data protection and the  right to privacy for all citizens are to be sunk into the ground.
An increase in security is not expected

“Send me a Whatsapp,” you hear (still) everywhere. Many citizens use  the chat apps every day, almost self-evident, of course, also send a  picture, a meme, an Internet link. Three quarters of 16- to 74 year olds  across the EU are registered with one of the various apps such as  Skype, Telegram, Threema, etc. In Germany, 60 million alone use the  WhatsApp chat service, which has been part of the Facebook Group Meta  for some time. Since that is the case, many have been looking for  alternatives because Facebook is considered a data vacuum cleaner with  partly dubary terms of use. Now the EU wants to put it equally on the  Big Tech Group and gain insight into the private communication of the  citizens, block it or prosecute it in the event of a case. The country  bloc seizes the technical services and becomes the imitator of the large  tech companies, which it should actually include in the sense of the  freedom of its citizens.

If the EU regulation comes, app users will probably see one of these  windows at some point. In it, they are asked whether they agree to  verify their sent images, photos and videos by artificial intelligence  (AI) or not. If not, they will no longer be able to use the service or  at least not send any pictures, etc. However, it is likely that many  will agree with the new terms of use almost otherwise – and so the EU  would come a little closer to the comprehensive control of its citizens.

Those who have something to hide will simply not agree to the new  conditions and use darker channels, as they do today. So there would be  no increase in security for small children who fall victim to sexual  abuse and whose images are then spread. Ultimately, the EU regulation  amounts to suspend mass surveillance of citizens and thus possible  prosecution even where there is no plaintiff. For example, where  teenagers send lewd pictures. And AI can, of course, become erred and  possibly classify harmless content as potentially dangerous.
Legal service of the Council: Arbitrary control violates fundamental rights

Initially, even the checking of the chat messages and recorded voice  messages was planned on keywords. These are individual regulations that  were withdrawn for the first, according to the former MEP Patrick Breyer  (Pirates). In addition, France has returned a derogation for security  authorities and military, which can then continue to send pictures and  videos without these being subjected to any kind of scanning.

The Legal Service of the Council was still in force on 24. May found  that "arbitrary chat control" is still on the EU agenda for persons who  are not suspected of committing a crime and, of course, constitute a  violation of fundamental rights (in Germany Article 13 of the Basic  Law).

If the regulation comes, private chat providers can no longer keep  one of their most important promises. Signal’s president, Meredith  Whittaker, writes in a recent press release that “upload moderation” is  only a new word for mass chat control: “There is no way to implement  such proposals related to end-to-end encrypted communication without  fundamentally undermining encryption and creating a dangerous weakness  in a core infrastructure that would have a global impact far beyond  Europe.”

The claim that content is still being “checked before” its encryption  is contrary to the end-to-end principle with which WhatsApp and signal  promote itself. Signal had once developed open source technology,  WhatsApp took it over, Mark Zuckerberg has not yet touched it. According  to Whittaker, encryption and “upload moderation” do not go together –  this is an “mathematical reality” that new words could not hide either.  The EU chat control proposal is about “mass scanning” about “the same  old monitoring with a new label” using “mass scanning”.

One thing goes without saying that if the chat services were to know  about “illegal activities” due to the surveillance of image content and  Internet addresses, they would not only have to inform the EU state or  supranational authorities immediately about it, but also “act quickly to  remove or block access to access it”. The AI-supported detection of  supposedly illegal content would therefore also result in its deletion.
Whittaker: We are previously leaving the EU market

Already in May, Whittaker announced that he would rely on the EU  market rather than engage in an undermining of encryption technology.  Now Signal has remained a niche provider with 40 million users  worldwide.

In addition to the head of the Signal, the Society for Freedom Rights also protest the organisation European Digital Rights (entitled “Be scanned – or get banned!”) and the Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Europe strongly against the draft regulation of the Belgian Presidency.

However, even the industry giant WhatsApp recently threatened with  its retirement from India within 60 days, according to the trade  magazines Rest of World and Inside Digital.  The government had previously adopted a regulation requiring  significant services (those with more than five million users) to  disclose the first author of information. With half a billion users in  India, WhatsApp belongs to this category, similar to what is a “very  large platform” under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and is  therefore subject to EU censorship law. Due to the importance of  WhatsApp for the Indian economy, a compromise is expected.

In the EU, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland  have been against the plans. Now the Belgians were apparently able to  capture France through the concession for security services and the  military. The blocking minority in the Council could therefore tip this  Wednesday. It is frightening that the conditions in the EU Council have  become so scarce that a majority is tangible. Estonia, Finland, Greece,  Italy, Portugal, Sweden, Slovenia and the Czech Republic have not yet  determined.

The European Parliament in Strasbourg-Brussels spoke out in November  to maintain chat encryption. If the Council decision is taken on  Wednesday, then perhaps the hour of this Parliament could really beat:  it would then have to do everything possible to prevent chat control in  the so-called 'trilogue' of the three EU institutions.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
🔴 A COMPLAINT HAS BEEN RECEIVED — NOW LET THE LAW TAKE ITS COURSE

A senior Supreme Court advocate, Adv. Bhanu Pratap Singh, has stated that a complaint has been submitted at Parliament Street Police Station concerning alleged violations relating to electoral processes and the conduct of public authorities.

According to the video, the complaint names several present and former Election Commission officials and other public functionaries, and alleges serious wrongdoing, including criminal conspiracy, fraud and other offences. These are allegations contained in the complaint, not established findings of guilt. The video also states that the police received the complaint and that further legal action may follow.

The appropriate democratic response is neither to dismiss such a complaint as “fake” nor to presume guilt before investigation.

If the allegations have no legal basis, the competent authorities should establish that through due process. If there is prima facie material disclosing an offence, the law should operate independently and impartially.

Electoral integrity is not a partisan issue. It concerns the constitutional rights of every citizen and the credibility of representative democracy.

At the same time, a complaint is not an FIR, an FIR is not proof of guilt, and an allegation is not a conviction. The rule of law requires both accountability and fairness.

What citizens can reasonably demand is:

✅ Transparent acknowledgment and processing of the complaint
✅ A reasoned decision by the competent police authority
✅ Independent and impartial investigation wherever legally warranted
✅ No political interference in the process
✅ Protection of evidence and relevant records
✅ Public accountability consistent with law and due process
✅ Respect for the constitutional rights of every citizen

Democracy is strengthened not when allegations are suppressed, but when credible allegations are examined through an independent legal process.

text:
The Pothole Is Not an Accident

On the morning of Saturday, 13 June 2026, a woman named Kantha was riding her two-wheeler along the Siddapur road near Marathahalli, dropping her daughter Neha at college. It had rained heavily the night before, and the potholes had filled with water, which is the detail that makes them invisible. She hit one, lost control and fell. A school bus coming from behind ran her over. She died on the road, in front of her daughter.

A case was registered at the Whitefield traffic police station. Against the bus.

That is the whole architecture of the problem in one line. There is always a vehicle to charge. There is never a road to charge.

Kantha's death was not a freak event. In Bengaluru it is closer to a season. The National Crime Records Bureau counts deaths caused by the negligence of civic bodies, meaning bad roads, potholes, open drains, collapsing infrastructure, electrocution. Bengaluru has ranked first among Indian metros in that category for six consecutive years. Delhi, bigger and denser and not famous for good roads, recorded four in a year when Bengaluru recorded seventeen. Either Bengaluru's roads are uniquely lethal, or every other city is better at not counting.

The national picture, in passing: figures tabled in Parliament record 9,438 people killed in pothole crashes between 2020 and 2024, about five a day, the toll rising 53% across those years. The Supreme Court called such numbers frightening as far back as 2018. Yet the same table shows Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Goa reporting zero pothole deaths in five years. Not zero potholes. Zero deaths. That is not a measurement. It is a filing decision.

A pothole death exists, legally, only if a police officer writes the word pothole into an FIR. Most do not. The crash becomes rash driving, or a hit-and-run. There is a driver to arrest and a section of the penal code that fits him. There is no section that fits an engineer who certified a road that dissolved in the first monsoon.

Bengaluru has a case that shows exactly how that works. On 6 February 2021, Tasdeeq Bushra, nineteen and in her first year of MBBS, was riding home along Hennur Main Road. She swerved to avoid a pothole. A truck hit her scooter from behind, she fell, and she went under the wheels.

The truck belonged to the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike. The city's own civic body owned the vehicle that killed her, and the road, and the pothole she was avoiding. The driver was arrested under Section 304A, causing death by negligence. The agency was not. Her father, Mushtaq Ahmed, put it better than any court has: "We have lost our only child. Whom will we pin the blame on? The vehicle was BBMP's and so was the driver, the roads were poorly built by them." BBMP, the water board and the electricity utility then blamed one another, which is the standard procedure.

Two details from what followed are worth sitting with. The FIR did not mention the pothole. And the pothole was filled within hours of her death. The evidence was repaired faster than the case was built.

Hers is not an outlier, it is the template. The News Minute traced thirteen pothole deaths in Bengaluru between 2017 and 2022. Families compensated: zero. Officials held accountable: zero. Not for want of a policy. BBMP had notified one, three lakh rupees for a death, and reporters found zonal chief engineers who did not know it existed and had never received a claim. A right nobody is told about is not a right, it is a press release. When Ashwin, twenty-seven, died on a pothole in MS Palya, police first blamed him for riding irresponsibly. His mother fought to get one line into the FIR naming unnamed civic officers. Nothing came of it.

The courts have been trying for a decade. A petition filed in 2015 is still running, and the High Court has reprimanded the corporation repeatedly, once issuing a contempt notice after BBMP resisted paying compensation at all. At one hearing, BBMP informed the court that Bengaluru contained 221 potholes in total. The court told it to be honest.

Then came the deadline. After a student named Dhanushree was crushed by a tipper lorry in September 2025 while swerving around a pothole, the Chief Minister announced that Bengaluru would be pothole-free by the end of October, with eleven hundred crore rupees sanctioned. Officials counted potholes by the thousand and announced them filled. The deadline was missed and replaced with another. In Whitefield, residents watched gravel tipped into holes, gravel that scatters as soon as vehicles pass over it.

Here is how that pothole-free year ended. On 20 November, three weeks after the deadline, Shantamma, forty-six, riding pillion home from work, fell on a broken stretch in Hulimavu and was run over by a truck. Police blamed potholes and loose gravel. On 17 December, Tabrez, thirty-two, swerved near Nelamangala and put his front wheel into an unbarricaded pipeline pit. He died at NIMHANS two days later. Not a pothole, strictly. The same disease.

Then the rains came back in June, and so did the holes, and so did Kantha's funeral.

The exhausting part is that the effort is real. The money is spent, the holes are counted and announced, and they return on schedule, because filling a pothole is not building a road. A pothole is the visible end of a chain: a specification diluted, a layer skipped, a bill cleared, an inspection signed. Every hole in a Bengaluru road has a name attached to it somewhere. None of those names ever reaches an FIR.

A drunk driver goes to jail. A negligent engineer gets transferred. A contractor whose road failed in ten weeks bids for the next tender. The person who dies becomes a line in a table.

Bengaluru has led that table for six years and has still not produced one official who lost a job over a death. Until a road failure is something a person can be charged with, the ritual continues: a monsoon, a hole, a two-wheeler, a bus behind it, a case against the driver, gravel by the weekend, and a family being told that what happened to them was an accident.

It was not an accident. Someone built that.

🔴 WHEN SENIOR CITIZENS ASK FOR BASIC SERVICES, THEY DESERVE RESPECT — NOT HUMILIATION

A senior citizen approaching public authorities for basic services should never have to feel that dignity is something they must beg for.

The video shared by @mshahi0024 raises a serious question about how citizens—particularly elderly citizens—are treated when they approach the state. The specific circumstances shown in the video should be independently verified, but the larger principle is indisputable: public officials and police are accountable to citizens, not the other way around.

India has dedicated mechanisms for senior-citizen protection. For example, Delhi Police's Senior Citizen Security Cell describes regular visits and security assistance for elderly citizens.

At the same time, the government and ruling party have been conducting extensive public events around the Prime Minister's birthday this year.

That contrast makes the question unavoidable:

What should come first—spectacle around political leadership, or dignity and responsive public services for ordinary citizens who have spent their lives contributing to the country?

Senior citizens do not need favours.

They need respect, accessible services, accountable officials and a state that listens.

A democracy is ultimately measured not by how its powerful are celebrated, but by how its most vulnerable citizens are treated when they knock on a government door.
